learning_objectives: Deconstruct a server-side request feature into input source, parser decomposition, DNS resolution, and connection sink.
Identify how ambient network authority (source IP position) allows an external actor to bypass network segmentation.
Formulate minimal, safe out-of-band and differential experiments to verify request primitives without destructive side-effects.
Calibrate SSRF capabilities from blind socket creation to cloud credential theft through structured capability chains.

safety_contract.authorization_assumption: Testing must only be conducted against systems and network ranges where explicit written authorization has been granted.
scope_constraints: Do not scan arbitrary RFC 1918 private subnets unless designated in engagement scope.
Do not access cloud credential paths (/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/) without explicit scoping approval.
stop_conditions: Halt execution if internal database contents, customer records, or production secrets are returned.
Do not execute mutating HTTP methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) against internal services.
safety_contract.safer_alternative: Request the metadata root directory (/latest/meta-data/) or localhost banner rather than sensitive internal resources.

applies_when: Application executes server-side HTTP/network requests based on user input.
Target server has network connectivity to internal, loopback, or cloud link-local endpoints not directly accessible to the user.
does_not_apply_when: Request fetching is performed strictly client-side by the user's browser.
Application server is completely isolated in an egress-filtered DMZ with no access to internal networks, localhost ports, or cloud metadata endpoints.
Cloud environment enforces IMDSv2 and application sink cannot craft custom HTTP PUT requests with required token headers.
variance_notes: In AWS, IMDSv1 permits simple GET requests, whereas IMDSv2 requires a token acquisition handshake via PUT with header X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds.
In GCP, the metadata service requires the 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' header, mitigating simple SSRF GET primitives unless header injection exists.
In Azure, the Instance Metadata Service requires the 'Metadata: true' header.

mental_model.one_sentence: SSRF occurs when an application that makes server-side network requests allows an attacker to influence the request destination, causing the server to use its privileged network position on the attacker's behalf.
mental_model.short_explanation: An application accepts input that determines where it sends a server-side network request. The server has a privileged network position — it can reach internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, and localhost services that external attackers cannot. When the attacker controls the destination, the server becomes an unwitting proxy: the request arrives at the target from a trusted internal IP, regardless of who initiated it. The attacker gains the server's network authority without gaining the server's identity.
mental_model.diagram:
Attacker
   │
   │ controls destination
   ▼
Application
   │
   │ makes request from trusted position
   ▼
Server-side HTTP client
   │
   ▼
Destination attacker cannot reach directly
   │
   ▼
Internal service / cloud metadata / localhost

analogy.text: You give a delivery address to an employee who has badge access to restricted buildings. The employee delivers your package to the address you specified — inside a building you cannot enter. The building's security checks the employee's badge, not your identity.
analogy.where_it_breaks: The analogy implies a single, predictable delivery. Real SSRF involves intermediate transformations (URL parsing, DNS resolution, HTTP redirects) that can change the effective destination after validation — as if the employee follows redirect signs to a different building after the address was already approved.

invariant.statement: Attacker-controlled input must not give an external actor unauthorized use of the server's network position.
invariant.why_it_matters: The server's network position is privileged — it includes access to internal networks, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), localhost services, and systems protected by network-layer access controls. Unauthorized use of this position allows reading internal data, stealing cloud credentials, interacting with internal services, and bypassing network segmentation.
invariant.violation_condition: Attacker-controlled input determines the destination of a server-side request without adequate validation, and the server makes the request using its privileged network position.
invariant.investigation_question: Can an external actor cause the server to make a network request to a destination the actor specifies, and does that destination include addresses the actor could not reach directly?

normal_behavior.description: The application fetches data from a predetermined, trusted backend URL. User input may influence query parameters or path segments, but the destination host is hardcoded or selected from a strict allowlist. The server's network position is not exposed to attacker control.
normal_behavior.diagram: User request → Application → Hardcoded backend URL → Trusted internal service → Response processed

vulnerable_behavior.description: The application accepts a user-supplied URL and passes it to a server-side HTTP client. The user controls the destination host. The server makes the request from its internal network position, crossing the trust boundary.
vulnerable_behavior.diagram:
Attacker-supplied URL → Application → Server HTTP client → Attacker's destination
                                                                    ↓
                                                        Internal service responds
                                                        to trusted internal IP

steps: 1. Attacker supplies a value (URL, hostname, IP) through an application input that influences a server-side request destination.
2. The application receives this value. It may validate, transform, or pass it through unchanged.
3. The value reaches a server-side HTTP client — the sink.
4. The HTTP client parses the URL (per RFC 3986 §3.2 for authority decomposition), resolves DNS, and initiates a connection.
5. The connection originates from the server's network interface. The destination sees a request from a trusted internal IP.
6. If the destination is an internal service, cloud metadata endpoint, or localhost service, it responds as if the request came from a legitimate internal component.
7. The attacker observes the result — response content (full SSRF), timing/error differences, or out-of-band callback (blind SSRF).

data_flow.source: User-controlled parameter (url, stockApi, webhook, callback, imageUrl, etc.)
data_flow.parser_or_component: Server-side HTTP client (urllib, requests, HttpClient, curl, server-side fetch)
data_flow.sink_or_decision: Outbound network connection from server's interface
data_flow.result: Request reaches restricted destination using server's network authority

trust_transformation.parser_or_interpreter: URL parser → DNS resolver → HTTP client
trust_transformation.authority_gained: Server's network position (internal reachability + ambient credentials)
trust_transformation.effect: Request to a destination the attacker cannot reach directly

conditions.condition: Attacker controls the destination (URL, hostname, or IP in a parameter that influences the request target)
conditions.how_to_test: Can you modify the parameter to specify an arbitrary URL?

conditions.condition: Input reaches a server-side request primitive (the value is passed to an HTTP client, not just stored or displayed)
conditions.how_to_test: Supply your callback server URL; does the server make a request?

conditions.condition: Server has a privileged network position (can reach destinations the attacker cannot)
conditions.how_to_test: Is the server on an internal network with access to internal services, metadata endpoints, or localhost?

conditions.condition: Restricted destination is reachable from the server
conditions.how_to_test: Can the server reach the target internal service/metadata endpoint?

conditions.condition: Response content returned to attacker (full-response SSRF)
conditions.how_to_test: Does the application display the fetched content?

conditions.condition: Out-of-band callback observable (blind SSRF with OOB)
conditions.how_to_test: Does your callback server receive a request from the server?

conditions.condition: Timing or error differences observable (blind inference)
conditions.how_to_test: Do response times or error messages differ for reachable vs. unreachable internal hosts?
Can the internal service be triggered to perform an observable action?

exploitability.gate_rule: If any AND condition is false, the attack path breaks. Within the OR group, at least one must be true for exploitability.

attack_surface: Any feature that accepts a URL as input (webhook config, URL preview, fetch-from-URL import, image URL, PDF generation from URL, API callback)
Parameters containing full or partial URLs (url=, stockApi=, callback=, next=, dest=, imageUrl=, path=)
Features that display or process remote content server-side
Data formats supporting URL references (XML with external entities, SVG with external references, HTML import)
HTTP headers that may influence server-side requests (Referer header used for analytics fetching)
Partial URL components in parameters (hostname-only, path-only) assembled server-side into a full URL

hypotheses.predicted_observation: Callback from your browser IP, not the server IP

hypotheses.hypothesis: URL is stored but never fetched

minimal_experiments.hypothesis: The application passes my input to a server-side HTTP client (H2)
minimal_experiments.experiment: Supply a URL pointing to a server you control (Burp Collaborator, webhook.site). Observe: does a request arrive, and from what source IP?
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: Callback from application server IP → H2 confirmed
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: Callback from browser IP (H1), proxy IP (H3), or no callback (H4)
minimal_experiments.information_gain: This single experiment distinguishes all four hypotheses.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If H2 confirmed → test internal destination reachability

minimal_experiments.hypothesis: The server can reach internal/restricted addresses
minimal_experiments.experiment: Supply http://127.0.0.1 or the cloud metadata root path http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (directory listing, not credential path). Observe response content, error, or timing difference.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: Response contains localhost content or metadata directory listing, OR error/timing pattern differs from external URLs
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: Same error as external URL / request blocked by validation
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Distinguishes 'server-side request exists' from 'server-side request can cross trust boundary'.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If blocked → investigate validation bypass (see defense_analysis). If accessible → determine impact by requesting specific internal endpoints (with authorization to demonstrate impact).

decision_points.question: Does the application accept a URL or hostname as input?
decision_points.no: Look for indirect URL influence: XML entities, partial URLs, Referer header, stored URLs in data formats

decision_points.question: Does the server make an outbound request when you supply a URL to your callback server?
decision_points.yes: Continue — you have a request primitive
decision_points.no: Input may not reach a request sink. Try different parameters, methods, encoding

decision_points.question: Does the request originate from the server's IP (not your browser)?
Can you direct the request to an internal/restricted address?
decision_points.yes: Continue — candidate SSRF with trust-boundary crossing
decision_points.no: Validation may be blocking. Investigate bypass (see defense_analysis)

decision_points.question: Can you observe the response, a side-effect, or an out-of-band signal?
decision_points.yes: Exploitable SSRF. Determine impact via capability chain
decision_points.no: Blind SSRF. Impact depends on triggerable side-effects

what_must_be_proven: The request originates from the server, not the client browser
The attacker can influence the destination
The destination includes addresses the attacker cannot reach directly
The result (response, timing, callback, or side-effect) is observable

evidence.evidence: Response contains content from an internal service (cloud metadata directory, internal admin panel HTML)
Out-of-band callback received from server IP when requesting an internal address
Timing/error differences between requests to internal vs. external destinations (connection refused for closed internal port vs. timeout)
Server makes request to external callback URL (proves server-side request, not internal reachability)
URL parameter exists in the application (does not prove it reaches a request sink)

confirmation.safe_confirmation: Point the URL parameter at your own callback server (Burp Collaborator). Verify the request arrives from the target application's server IP. Then test the metadata root path (/latest/meta-data/) which returns a directory listing — not credentials. Credential retrieval (/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>) should be a deliberate impact-demonstration step after confirming the vulnerability and having explicit authorization.

capability_and_impact.primitive: Server-side request to an attacker-controlled destination from the server's network position

capabilities.additional_prerequisite: Internal services are running and accessible from the server's network
capabilities.impact: Can reach internal APIs, admin panels, databases

capabilities.additional_prerequisite: Full-response SSRF (response content returned to attacker)

Cloud environment with metadata service enabled. IMDSv1 allows simple GET requests to the metadata endpoint. IMDSv2 blocks this in two ways: (1) it requires a PUT request with a custom header to get a token first — most SSRF primitives only support GET, so they cannot obtain the token, and (2) the default hop limit (TTL=1) means the token request packet expires before crossing a network boundary, so SSRF from inside a container cannot even reach the metadata endpoint. These defenses protect credentials specifically, not internal network access generally.
capabilities.impact: If IMDSv1 or bypassable IMDSv2: IAM role credential theft

capabilities.capability: Cloud account actions using stolen credentials
capabilities.additional_prerequisite: IAM role has meaningful permissions (S3 access, EC2 control, etc.)
capabilities.impact: Cloud account compromise proportional to role permissions

impact_conditions: Whether response content is returned (full vs. blind)
What internal services are reachable from the server
Whether internal services require authentication from the server's IP
Whether the server has ambient credentials (cloud IAM roles, service accounts)
Whether IMDSv1 or IMDSv2 is in use (IMDSv2 blocks most SSRF credential theft)
Whether the attacker can chain SSRF with other vulnerabilities

defense_analysis.assumption: All representations of internal IP addresses are covered by the blocklist.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The blocklist must account for every possible representation that the HTTP client will resolve to an internal IP: decimal (2130706433), octal (017700000001), hex (0x7f000001), IPv6 (::1, ::ffff:127.0.0.1), abbreviated (127.1), and any other format the URL parser or DNS resolver accepts.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Alternative IP representations bypass string-matching blocklists. DNS rebinding changes the resolved IP after validation. Redirects change the destination after validation.
defense_analysis.investigation: Can I find a representation of an internal IP that the blocklist does not recognize but the HTTP client resolves correctly?

defense_analysis.defense: Hostname allowlist (only permit requests to known external domains)
defense_analysis.assumption: The hostname in the URL unambiguously identifies the destination, and allowed hostnames cannot be manipulated to reach internal addresses.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The URL parser correctly extracts the hostname. DNS resolution of allowed hostnames returns only external IPs. No open redirects exist on allowed domains.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: URL parsing tricks (RFC 3986 §3.2.1 — userinfo@host makes the host the part after '@'). DNS rebinding of allowed hostnames. Open redirects on allowed domains redirect to internal URLs after the allowlist check passes.
defense_analysis.investigation: Can I manipulate which part of the URL the validator considers the hostname? Can I exploit an open redirect on an allowed domain? Can I make an allowed hostname resolve to an internal IP?

defense_analysis.defense: Validate resolved IP address (resolve DNS, then check the IP against internal ranges before connecting)
defense_analysis.assumption: The IP resolved during validation is the same IP the HTTP client will connect to.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: DNS resolution must not change between validation and connection (no rebinding). The HTTP client must not re-resolve DNS. The connection must go to the validated IP, not a different one.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: DNS rebinding with very short TTL (0s) — first resolution returns a public IP, second returns an internal IP. Some HTTP client libraries re-resolve DNS on redirect or connection retry.
defense_analysis.investigation: Can I demonstrate that the validation and connection steps observe different DNS resolutions? Does the HTTP client re-resolve on redirect?

defense_analysis.defense: Network segmentation (firewall rules, security groups restricting server egress to internal networks)
defense_analysis.assumption: The application server cannot reach sensitive internal services regardless of application-layer behavior.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: Firewall/security-group rules must block the application server from reaching internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, and localhost services on other ports.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Overly permissive egress rules. Metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) not blocked. Internal services on the same host accessible via localhost.
defense_analysis.investigation: What egress rules apply to the application server? Is the metadata endpoint reachable? Are other services running on localhost?

common_misconceptions.why_wrong: SSRF exploits the server's entire network position — internal APIs, adjacent services, cloud metadata, any restricted destination. Localhost is one target, not the definition.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: The vulnerability is destination control + privileged network position. Any restricted destination is relevant.

common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Blind SSRF does not return response content. The primitive still exists — the server makes the request — but the attacker must rely on OOB callbacks, timing, errors, or side-effects.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: Full vs. blind is a spectrum of observability, not a binary. Each variant requires different investigation techniques.

common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Cloud credential theft requires: cloud environment, metadata endpoint accessible, IMDSv1 (or IMDSv2 bypass), IAM role attached, and role with meaningful permissions. Each is an additional prerequisite in the capability chain.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: Impact depends on the capability chain. SSRF is the primitive — impact depends on what's reachable and what authority those services grant.

common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Blocklists are bypassable via DNS rebinding, alternative IP representations (decimal, octal, hex, IPv6), redirects, URL parsing disagreements, and double-encoding.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: Blocklists create a cat-and-mouse game because the assumption 'all malicious representations are blocked' is hard to guarantee. Allowlists are more robust because they require the destination to match a known-good pattern.

false_positives.observation: URL parameter exists in the request
false_positives.why_incorrect: The URL may be used for display, logging, or client-side redirect — never passed to a server-side request primitive.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Send a callback-server URL; check if the server actually makes a request to it.

false_positives.why_incorrect: The fetch may be client-side (browser JavaScript). No trust boundary is crossed if the browser makes the request.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Check the source IP at your callback server: application server IP vs. your browser IP.

false_positives.observation: Server makes request to your callback URL
false_positives.why_incorrect: Server-side request exists, but SSRF requires crossing the trust boundary to a restricted destination. If all internal addresses are blocked by effective validation, the invariant is preserved.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Test internal destination reachability (127.0.0.1, metadata IP, internal hostnames).

failed_attempts.attempt: Supply http://127.0.0.1 directly in the URL parameter
failed_attempts.why: Application validates against an internal-IP blocklist before making the request. Validation occurs before the sink.
failed_attempts.lesson: The defense assumption is 'all internal IP representations are blocked.' Investigate whether the validator and sink interpret the destination differently — URL parsing tricks, DNS rebinding, redirects, alternative IP representations.

failed_attempts.attempt: Use DNS rebinding (short-TTL hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1)
failed_attempts.why: Application validates the resolved IP (not the hostname) or re-resolves DNS after initial validation. The defense assumption 'DNS is stable between check and connect' is correctly protected.
failed_attempts.lesson: Defense validates at the correct layer — resolved IP, not hostname string. This is effective. Try other approaches: redirect chains, URL parsing disagreements, scheme switching.

variants.name: Full-response SSRF
variants.condition: The application returns the fetched content to the attacker in the HTTP response.
variants.mechanism_detail: The attacker can read the full response from internal services. This is the highest-impact variant because internal data (admin panels, metadata credentials, API responses) is directly observable.
variants.investigation_difference: Standard investigation: supply internal URL, read response. The response content itself proves the trust boundary was crossed.
variants.how_to_identify: Supply your callback server URL and check if the response body appears in the application's response.
variants.how_to_confirm: Request the cloud metadata root path (169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/) and verify the response contains the metadata directory listing.

variants.name: Blind SSRF
variants.condition: The application makes the server-side request but does not return the response content to the attacker.
variants.mechanism_detail: The SSRF primitive exists — the server makes the request — but the attacker cannot read the response. Impact depends on: (1) OOB callbacks confirming the request was made, (2) timing/error differences revealing internal network topology, (3) triggerable side-effects on internal services (e.g., POST to internal admin APIs that perform state changes).
variants.investigation_difference: Cannot read response content. Must use: (a) Burp Collaborator / OOB callback to confirm the request reaches attacker-controlled or internal destinations. (b) Timing analysis: requests to open internal ports may return faster than requests to closed ports or external hosts. (c) Error-message differences between reachable and unreachable internal hosts. (d) Side-effect observation: if the internal service performs an action on receipt of the SSRF request.
variants.how_to_identify: Application does not display fetched content, but your callback server receives requests from the server IP when you supply URLs.
variants.how_to_confirm: Timing/error difference: compare response time for http://127.0.0.1:80 (likely fast — service exists) vs. http://127.0.0.1:9999 (likely timeout — no service). Consistent timing difference suggests the server is making the request and reaching the destination.

transfer.shared_mechanism: Trust-boundary confusion: attacker-controlled input causes a privileged component to use its network authority on the attacker's behalf.

related_topics.shared_principle: XML external entities trigger server-side requests — SSRF via the XML parser as the input vector rather than a direct URL parameter.
redirect_uri manipulation exploits URL validation gaps similar to SSRF URL validation bypasses. Both depend on the concepts of URL parsing and allowlist enforcement.

transfer.transferable_reasoning: Look for any feature where: (1) user input influences a destination [concept.url-parsing], (2) a server-side component makes a request using that destination [concept.network-trust-boundaries], and (3) the request can reach destinations the attacker cannot access directly. The specific features below are examples of applying this reasoning.

PDF/image generators fetching remote resources
File import from URL
API proxy / gateway URL parameters
Headless browser screenshot/rendering services
Document processors (DOCX, SVG with external references)

RSS/Atom feed fetchers
Link preview / URL unfurling features
Cloud function triggers with URL parameters

sources.title: RFC 3986 - Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
sources.claim: Defines URI syntax including authority component §3.2 (userinfo@host:port decomposition), §3.2.1 (User Information and '@' delimiter), §2.1 (Percent-Encoding). These are directly relevant to URL parsing disagreements exploitable in SSRF filter bypasses.

sources.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy - Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
sources.claim: Defines SSRF as causing the server to make requests to unintended locations. Documents trust relationships, attacks against server/backend systems, blocklist/allowlist bypass techniques, blind SSRF, and hidden attack surface (partial URLs, data formats, Referer header).

sources.title: OWASP - Server Side Request Forgery
sources.claim: Describes SSRF as abusing server functionality to perform requests to internal/external resources on behalf of the server.

sources.title: OWASP - Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Documents SSRF prevention: application-layer validation (allowlists over blocklists, validate after DNS resolution), network-layer controls (egress filtering, segmentation), defense-in-depth. Documents DNS rebinding as bypass.

sources.title: AWS - Instance metadata and user data
sources.claim: EC2 instance metadata at 169.254.169.254. IMDSv1 allows GET; IMDSv2 requires PUT with X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds header for token, then GET with X-aws-ec2-metadata-token header. IAM credentials at /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name>.

sources.title: CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
sources.claim: Defines SSRF as a weakness where the web server receives a URL or similar request and retrieves contents without ensuring it is sent to the expected destination.

sources.title: Orange Tsai - A New Era of SSRF (BlackHat USA 2017)
sources.claim: Documents URL parser disagreements across programming languages (Python, PHP, NodeJS, Ruby, Java) enabling SSRF filter bypasses via inconsistent authority decomposition and scheme handling.

claims.statement: RFC 3986 §3.2 defines the URI authority component as [userinfo@]host[:port], meaning that in 'user@host', 'host' is the string following the '@' delimiter, not preceding it.
Resolving DNS during validation and resolving DNS again during HTTP socket connection creates a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability exploitable via DNS rebinding (TTL: 0s).
claims.scope: Applications that validate hostnames via DNS resolution but pass the original hostname string to the HTTP client sink

claims.statement: Network-segmented internal microservices and cloud metadata endpoints grant ambient authorization based on source IP address rather than requiring per-request cryptographic authentication.
claims.scope: Cloud instances and private VPC networks relying solely on perimeter network controls

claims.statement: AWS IMDSv2 requires a PUT request with a custom header to acquire a session token, thereby neutralizing simple GET-only SSRF primitives. Additionally, the default hop limit (TTL=1) on the token request prevents it from crossing a network boundary — so SSRF from inside a container cannot reach the metadata endpoint even if the primitive supports PUT with custom headers.
claims.scope: AWS EC2 instances with IMDSv2 enabled. The hop limit defense specifically applies when the SSRF originates from a container or crosses a network boundary.

claims.statement: Server-side HTTP client libraries that follow HTTP 3xx redirects automatically will connect to the target specified in the Location header without re-applying application-layer input allowlists.
claims.scope: Default configurations of standard HTTP client libraries (e.g. requests, curl, urllib)

claims.statement: Some socket libraries resolve alternative IP integer representations (such as dword/decimal 2130706433 or octal 017700000001) to 127.0.0.1, bypassing naive regex-based IP blocklists. However, support varies: glibc accepts octal/hex/decimal, but musl libc (Alpine Linux/Docker), Go's net.ParseIP(), and Python's ipaddress module do not.
claims.scope: glibc-based resolvers (Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL). Does NOT reliably apply to musl-based systems (Alpine Linux), Go standard library, or Python ipaddress module.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Given an unfamiliar application feature that takes a URL, derive a set of mutually exclusive hypotheses to determine whether fetching occurs client-side, via server-side proxy, or via third-party CDN.
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Learner designs an out-of-band listener test that distinguishes client, server, and third-party IP sources in one experiment.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Evaluate an application-layer defense against SSRF and identify the underlying assumption that causes it to fail (e.g. DNS rebinding, redirect following, or URI parser disagreement).
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Learner explains the specific TOCTOU or parser discrepancy enabling the bypass rather than guessing payloads.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Calibrate the established capability of an SSRF primitive against downstream impact without overstating conclusions.
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Learner cleanly distinguishes between network reachability, response observability, and cloud credential acquisition.

scenarios.title: Containerized Headless Browser Rendering to Internal gRPC

prompt.setup: A thumbnail generation microservice accepts a POST parameter `target_url`. Inside a Kubernetes pod, the service launches headless Chromium with `--no-sandbox` to render the page, saves a PNG screenshot to an S3 bucket, and returns a pre-signed S3 URL to the client. The HTTP response body of the target URL is never returned to the caller. Network policies allow the pod to initiate outbound TCP connections to an internal payment service running gRPC on `10.244.3.15:8443` and to external internet hosts.
prompt.task_question: Analyze this architecture: (1) What capability has the attacker established? (2) What remains unproven or constrained? (3) Propose the minimal safe experiment to advance the investigation without risking state corruption on the payment service.

expected_reasoning.invariant_analysis: The security invariant requires that external users cannot utilize the container's privileged internal network position to reach restricted services (the internal gRPC service or metadata endpoints).
expected_reasoning.boundary_analysis: The trust boundary is crossed when Chromium in the container initiates connections from its internal pod IP (`10.244.x.x`) to `10.244.3.15:8443`, an internal endpoint unreachable from the public internet.
competing_hypotheses: Hypothesis A: Chromium can establish TCP connections and render internal HTTP/HTTPS responses into the screenshot (visual exfiltration).
Hypothesis B: The payment service strictly speaks gRPC (HTTP/2 with protocol buffers) and will immediately reject/reset HTTP/1.1 requests from Chromium without rendering.
Hypothesis C: Network egress policies on the pod drop packets destined for internal RFC 1918 subnets, neutralizing the primitive.
expected_reasoning.minimal_safe_experiment: Point `target_url` to an attacker-controlled external web server serving HTML that attempts an `` fetch to `http://10.244.3.15:8443/` while capturing DNS/TCP callback telemetry, and inspect the generated screenshot for browser error messages (e.g. ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED vs ERR_SSL_PROTOCOL_ERROR vs valid render).
expected_reasoning.capability_calibration: The established primitive is blind SSRF via a full browser engine. The attacker has NOT established gRPC command execution, internal data reading, or credential theft; those depend on protocol compatibility and visual capture.
expected_reasoning.remaining_uncertainties: Unknown whether JavaScript execution is enabled in Chromium; unknown whether gRPC responds to HTTP GET; unknown whether metadata IP is reachable from container network.

scoring_rubric.description: Ability to identify the protected security guarantee and its violation condition.

levels.0: Fails to identify any invariant; discusses general hacking tools or wordlists.
levels.1: Mentions that SSRF is bad or that internal networks should be private.
levels.2: Identifies that the container's network position is being used to reach internal addresses.
levels.3: Explicitly articulates that external input must not grant unauthorized network access to internal pod-reachable services.
levels.4: Formulates the exact invariant and defines the operational violation condition in terms of ambient pod authority.

scoring_rubric.description: Accuracy in mapping untrusted input through components to the trusted boundary.

levels.0: Does not understand where the request originates or assumes client browser makes the request.
levels.1: Recognizes that the container makes the request but confuses Kubernetes networking with local machine.
levels.2: Identifies the boundary between external internet and internal cluster IP space (10.244.x.x).
levels.3: Accurately traces flow: parameter -> microservice -> Chromium instance -> pod interface -> internal service.
levels.4: Traces full boundary flow and explicitly identifies ambient network authority granted to pod IP by cluster network policies.

scoring_rubric.description: Formulation of falsifiable, mutually exclusive competing hypotheses.

levels.0: No hypotheses formulated; assumes instant total compromise.
levels.1: Single hypothesis that the service is vulnerable without alternative possibilities.
levels.2: Proposes two hypotheses but they are not clearly distinguished.
levels.3: Proposes distinct hypotheses covering network reachability vs protocol incompatibility (gRPC vs HTTP).
levels.4: Proposes comprehensive, mutually exclusive hypotheses accounting for network policies, protocol compatibility, and visual rendering.

scoring_rubric.description: Selection of minimal, non-destructive experiments producing maximum information gain.

levels.0: Proposes sending destructive payloads, brute forcing, or spamming gRPC methods.
levels.1: Proposes generic SSRF payloads from cheatsheets without regard for target architecture.
levels.2: Proposes using a callback server but does not address gRPC specificity.
levels.3: Designs a safe test using an attacker-controlled page to observe browser behavior and screenshot error codes.
levels.4: Designs a minimal, non-destructive test isolating network reachability from protocol parsing, with explicit stop conditions.

scoring_rubric.description: Strict separation between demonstrated primitive and hypothetical impact.

levels.0: Equates thumbnail URL acceptance with full database takeover or remote code execution.
levels.1: Claims full SSRF without noting that response bodies are never returned to the caller.
levels.2: Identifies blind SSRF but assumes visual screenshot exfiltration is guaranteed.
levels.3: Accurately states that only an outbound browser request primitive has been proven, while data extraction remains conditional.
levels.4: Rigorously separates the primitive (browser navigation) from capabilities (visual leakage vs blind gRPC interaction) and impact (payment compromise).

scoring_rubric.description: Identification of unknown factors that require further testing before drawing conclusions.

levels.0: Expresses complete certainty based on assumptions.
levels.1: Acknowledges that something might fail but cannot specify what.
levels.2: Notes that gRPC might not work with HTTP.
levels.3: Clearly lists unproven assumptions: protocol compatibility, JS execution flags, egress rules.
levels.4: Formulates an exhaustive matrix of open uncertainties with corresponding validation steps for each.

common_learner_errors.error: Assuming gRPC can be exploited like a standard HTTP REST API
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: gRPC uses HTTP/2 with binary framing (Protobuf). Sending an HTTP/1.1 GET from a browser URL bar often yields a 400 Bad Request or connection termination rather than valid RPC execution.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Study concept.network-trust-boundaries and note how transport layer reachability differs from application layer compatibility.

common_learner_errors.error: Declaring critical impact immediately upon discovering the URL parameter
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: Blind SSRF in an isolated container without access to cloud metadata or with strict firewall rules may have negligible practical impact.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Follow the capability chain: primitive -> reachability -> observable capability -> impact.

DIAGRAM 3: CAUSAL CHAIN & DATA FLOW
===============================================================================

[ ATTACKER DATA ]
  Source: Raw string input in HTTP parameter, JSON payload, or header
  Example: "http://attacker-controlled-host:80/path"
        │
        ▼
[ TRANSFORMATION LAYER ]
  1. Parameter parsing & URL decoding (%2f -> /, %40 -> @)
  2. Optional Validation check (flawed allowlist, blocklist, or regex)
        │
        ▼
[ PARSER INTERPRETATION (RFC 3986 §3.2) ]
  HTTP Client decomposes URI:
    Scheme:    "http"
    Authority: [userinfo@]host[:port]
    Path:      "/path"
        │
        ▼
[ RESOLUTION LAYER (DNS) ]
  Operating system / resolver resolves hostname to IP address (A/AAAA record):
  - Normal: "example.com" -> 93.184.216.34
  - Rebinding: "rebind.com" -> 93.184.216.34 (at check) -> 127.0.0.1 (at connect)
        │
        ▼
[ SINK / ACTION PRIMITIVE ]
  Kernel socket execution:
  - connect(socket_fd, { sockaddr_in: 127.0.0.1:80 }, ...)
  - Outbound TCP/TLS handshake executed with SERVER's IP as source IP
        │
        ▼
[ UNINTENDED INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY CROSSING ]
  Destination server evaluates packet:
  - Source IP is within local loopback or VPC subnet
  - Destination assumes caller is internal / trusted (ambient authority)
        │
        ▼
[ EFFECT & OBSERVABILITY ]
  - Full SSRF: Internal response passed back to attacker
  - Blind SSRF (OOB): Destination or external callback logs connection
  - Blind SSRF (Inference): Socket timeout vs. connection refused timing differences
  - Blind SSRF (Side-Effect): Internal state modified (e.g., admin action executed)
===============================================================================

DIAGRAM 4: EXPLOITABILITY BOOLEAN LOGIC GATES
===============================================================================

For SSRF to be practically exploitable, all mandatory conditions must evaluate
to TRUE (AND gates), and at least one observability path must exist (OR gate).

                     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                     │ C1: Attacker controls destination parameter     │
                     └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                              ▼ [AND]
                     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                     │ C2: Input reaches server-side request primitive  │
                     │     (passed to HTTP client / socket sink)        │
                     └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                              ▼ [AND]
                     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                     │ C3: Server possesses privileged network position │
                     │     (e.g., inside VPC, loopback access, IMDS)    │
                     └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                              ▼ [AND]
                     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                     │ C4: Restricted destination is network reachable  │
                     │     (not blocked by host firewall/egress filter) │
                     └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                              ▼ [AND]
    ══════════════════════════════════════════╪════════════════════════════════════
                             AT LEAST ONE MUST BE TRUE [OR]
    ══════════════════════════════════════════╪════════════════════════════════════
            ┌───────────────┬─────────────────┴───────────────┬──────────────┐
            ▼               ▼                                 ▼              ▼
     ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐                   ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐
     │ E1: Full    │ │ E2: Out-of- │                   │ E3: Timing/ │ │ E4: State-  │
     │ response    │ │ band (OOB)  │                   │ Error       │ │ changing    │
     │ returned to │ │ callback    │                   │ Differential│ │ side-effect │
     │ attacker    │ │ received    │                   │ Observable  │ │ triggered   │
     └──────┬──────┘ └──────┬──────┘                   └──────┬──────┘ └──────┬──────┘
            │               │                                 │               │
            └───────────────┴─────────────────┬───────────────┴───────────────┘

                             └──────────────────────────────────┘

GATE FAILURE MODES:
- If C1 is FALSE (destination strictly fixed): No SSRF possible.
- If C2 is FALSE (parameter only saved to DB or reflected): Input validation / XSS perhaps, not SSRF.
- If C3 is FALSE (server has zero privileged access; isolated DMZ): No security boundary crossed.
- If C4 is FALSE (egress gateway drops packet to 10.0.0.0/8 & 169.254.169.254): Invariant holds.
- If ALL E1-E4 are FALSE: Silent void request; primitive exists but yields zero capability.

SCENARIO A: RFC 3986 §3.2 AUTHORITY DISAGREEMENT (USERINFO VS HOST)

Input: "http://allowed-domain.com@127.0.0.1:80/admin"

  FLAWED VALIDATOR / NAIVE REGEX          RFC 3986 COMPLIANT HTTP CLIENT
  (e.g., ^http[s]?://allowed-domain\.com) (Sink: curl, requests, urllib)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Matches prefix:                  │    │ Authority decomposition (§3.2):  │
  │ "allowed-domain.com"             │    │ userinfo = "allowed-domain.com"  │
  │                                  │    │ delimiter = "@"                  │
  │ Decision:                        │    │ host     = "127.0.0.1"           │
  │ Matches allowlist -> PERMITTED   │    │ port     = "80"                  │
  └────────────────┬─────────────────┘    │                                  │

                   │                      │ Connect to host: 127.0.0.1:80    │
                   │                      └────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                   ▼                                       ▼
             ALLOWLIST PASSED                      CONNECTS TO LOCALHOST


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SCENARIO B: TIME-OF-CHECK / TIME-OF-USE (DNS REBINDING)

Host controlled by attacker: "rebind.attacker.com" (TTL: 0 seconds)

  TIME T0: VALIDATION CHECK                TIME T1: CONNECTION SINK
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Application resolves hostname:   │    │ HTTP Client connects to hostname:│
  │ gethostbyname("rebind...")       │    │ gethostbyname("rebind...")       │
  │                                  │    │                                  │
  │ Attacker DNS returns:            │    │ Attacker DNS returns (new TTL):  │
  │ IP: 93.184.216.34 (Public IP)    │    │ IP: 169.254.169.254 (IMDS IP)    │
  │                                  │    │                                  │
  │ Validation Logic:                │    │ Client Socket:                   │
  │ Is 93.184.216.34 private? NO.    │    │ connect(socket, 169.254.169.254) │
  │ Status: ALLOWED                  │    │ Status: CONNECTED                │
  └────────────────┬─────────────────┘    └────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                   │                                       │
                   ▼                                       ▼
             IP IS PUBLIC                         REQUEST REACHES IMDS

ROOT CAUSE:
The validator and the sink do not share the same interpretation of the input!
In Scenario A: Disagreement on URI syntax decomposition.
In Scenario B: Disagreement on the temporal resolution of the hostname.

learning_objectives: Deconstruct a state-changing web action into transport method, credential attachment mechanism, and origin verification sink.
Contrast the Same-Origin Policy's permissive cross-origin write rules against its restrictive read rules to identify why CSRF succeeds.
Formulate minimal, safe non-destructive experiments to verify whether an endpoint enforces anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookie policies.
Calibrate CSRF exploitability across browser environments, distinguishing between SameSite=None, SameSite=Lax navigations, and 2-minute Lax windows.

safety_contract.authorization_assumption: Testing must only be conducted against systems, web domains, and account profiles where explicit written authorization has been granted by the application owner.
scope_constraints: Do not trigger state mutations (e.g. email change, password update, fund transfer) against user accounts not owned by the assessment team.
Conduct all cross-site verification experiments between two dedicated, tester-controlled accounts (e.g., tester-victim and tester-attacker).
Do not host public CSRF demonstration pages that can be triggered by unauthenticated third parties or internet crawlers.
safety_contract.data_exposure_risk: low (elevated to medium for Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking variants, where the attacker gains bidirectional read/write access to the authenticated socket stream)
stop_conditions: Halt testing immediately if an action inadvertently mutates production data or affects real customer accounts.
Do not perform destructive state changes (e.g., account deletion, irreversible balance transfer, administrative permission elevation) during automated verification.
safety_contract.safer_alternative: Target a benign, idempotent, or easily reversible state change (such as updating a cosmetic profile bio or adding a test tag) rather than critical authentication or financial endpoints.

applies_when: The application relies on ambient credentials (session cookies, HTTP Basic/Digest authentication, or TLS client certificates) to identify authenticated users.
The target endpoint executes a state-changing operation (data mutation, transaction, account configuration change) upon receiving an HTTP request.
The endpoint lacks an unpredictable, origin-bound proof of user intent (anti-CSRF token) or does not validate it correctly.
does_not_apply_when: The application uses an explicit, non-ambient authorization mechanism (such as an 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' header stored in JavaScript memory or Web Storage) that the browser never attaches automatically to cross-site requests.
All session cookies are configured with 'SameSite=Strict', preventing the browser from attaching them to any cross-site request, including top-level navigations.
The endpoint is strictly read-only and idempotent (RFC 7231 safe methods) with no state-changing side-effects.
The server enforces strict Fetch Metadata policies (Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin) across all incoming requests before processing business logic.
variance_notes: In modern Chromium browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave), cookies that omit the SameSite attribute default to 'SameSite=Lax'. Cross-site form POST requests omit these cookies, mitigating traditional form CSRF unless the cookie was set within the past 120 seconds ('Lax-allowing-unsafe' window).
Safari and Firefox enforce strict Lax or intelligent tracking prevention boundaries that may drop cross-site cookies regardless of explicit flags in third-party contexts.
Mobile web applications embedded within native WebViews (Android WebView, iOS WKWebView) may lack default SameSite=Lax enforcement unless explicitly configured by the mobile developer.
Endpoints performing state mutations on HTTP GET remain vulnerable across all browsers even under SameSite=Lax, because top-level GET navigations always transmit Lax cookies.

mental_model.one_sentence: CSRF occurs when a web application executes a state-changing action based solely on ambient session credentials, allowing an untrusted external website to trick the user's browser into submitting an unauthorized request on the user's behalf.
mental_model.short_explanation: When you visit a website, your browser saves your login session in cookies. By design, whenever your browser sends a request to that website, it automatically includes those cookies—this is 'ambient authority'. An attacker hosts a malicious web page that quietly sends a request to your bank or email provider. Because the Same-Origin Policy permits cross-origin request dispatch, your browser sends the request along with your real login cookies. The destination server sees your valid cookies and assumes you intended to perform the action, executing the attacker's commands using your privileges.
mental_model.diagram:
Attacker Web Page (evil.com)
   │
   │ 1. Coerces request dispatch (<form>, fetch)
   ▼
Victim's Browser Engine (Confused Deputy)
   │
   │ 2. Automatically attaches Cookie: session=xyz
   ▼
Vulnerable Target Application (bank.com)
   │
   │ 3. Validates session cookie, omits origin validation
   ▼
State Mutation Executed (Transfer funds / change email)

analogy.text: A company courier wears an official badge that automatically unlocks the security doors at the corporate headquarters. An imposter hands the courier a sealed envelope stamped with legitimate internal markings, asking the courier to hand it to the wire transfer desk. When the courier arrives, the security guards recognize the courier's official badge, let the courier through, and the wire desk processes the transfer order in the envelope—without checking whether the corporate account holder actually drafted it.
analogy.where_it_breaks: In the physical world, a human teller can inspect the courier, notice strange behavior, or demand an interactive signature. In the browser runtime, the HTTP client attaches the identical binary cookie string without any human hesitation, and standard HTTP requests carry no visual indicator of coercion unless the application explicitly validates cryptographic nonces or modern Fetch Metadata headers.

invariant.statement: A state-changing action must not be executed without verifying that the request was intentionally initiated by the user within the authentic application context.
invariant.why_it_matters: Ambient credentials (session cookies) identify WHO the user is, but they do NOT prove WHAT CONTEXT generated the request. Without verifying request intentionality and origin provenance, any untrusted website visited by the user can commandeer the user's authenticated session, performing unauthorized financial transfers, password resets, account takeovers, and configuration changes.
invariant.violation_condition: An endpoint executes a state mutation upon receiving an HTTP request that carries valid ambient credentials, but lacks verification of an unpredictable, unforgeable origin-bound token or trusted origin metadata header.
invariant.investigation_question: Can an external origin cause the authenticated victim's browser to submit a request to this endpoint that successfully mutates server-side state, without the external origin knowing or guessing an unforgeable secret?

normal_behavior.description: The user interacts with the authentic application interface (e.g. loads https://app.example.com/settings). The application renders an HTML form or client-side component containing a unique, cryptographically random anti-CSRF token tied to the user's active session. When the user deliberately clicks 'Save Changes', the browser dispatches a same-origin POST request containing both the ambient session cookie and the anti-CSRF token. The server validates both the session cookie and the anti-CSRF token before applying the changes.
normal_behavior.diagram: User Interface (app.example.com) → Deliberate form submission → Dispatches POST with Cookie AND anti-CSRF token → Server verifies both → State mutation succeeds

vulnerable_behavior.description: The target endpoint accepts state-changing requests relying exclusively on ambient cookies for authorization, without requiring or verifying an unforgeable anti-CSRF token. An attacker tricks the victim into visiting a malicious site (https://evil.com). The attacker's page automatically submits a hidden form or issues a request targeting the vulnerable endpoint. The victim's browser automatically appends the victim's session cookies. The server validates the session cookie and applies the state mutation, unaware that the request was initiated by evil.com.
vulnerable_behavior.diagram: Victim visits evil.com → Script auto-submits hidden form targeting app.example.com → Browser appends ambient session cookie → Target server sees valid session → State mutation executes without user consent

steps: 1. The victim establishes an authenticated session with the target application, which sets an ambient session cookie in the browser's cookie jar.
2. The victim, while keeping the session active, navigates to an attacker-controlled web page (e.g. via phishing, malicious advertisement, or compromised forum).
3. The attacker's page executes client-side code that initiates an HTTP request targeting a sensitive, state-changing endpoint on the target application.

4. The victim's browser processes the outbound request. Because the request destination matches the target application's domain, the browser automatically attaches the matching session cookies (ambient credentials).
5. The target application receives the request, parses the Cookie header, locates the valid session, and executes the requested state change.

6. The response is returned to the browser. Even though the Same-Origin Policy prevents the attacker's script on evil.com from reading the response body, the server-side state change is already committed.

data_flow.source: Attacker-controlled HTML page or script specifying operation parameters (e.g., new_email=attacker@evil.com)
transformations: Browser DOM parsing of form or fetch() call
Cookie jar lookup matching destination domain and path
Ambient credential injection into HTTP Cookie header
Transport across network to target server
data_flow.parser_or_component: Target web server HTTP routing and session middleware
data_flow.sink_or_decision: Application business logic endpoint executing database mutations or account updates
data_flow.result: State mutation executed under victim's identity without victim intent

trust_transformation.attacker_data: Arbitrary parameter values for a state-changing action (recipient, amount, email address)
trust_transformation.parser_or_interpreter: Victim's web browser HTTP engine + Target web application session validator
trust_transformation.new_meaning: An authenticated, authorized instruction issued by the legitimate account owner
trust_transformation.authority_gained: Victim's personal account authority and application permissions
trust_transformation.effect: Execution of privileged transactions without victim knowledge or consent

conditions.condition: The target endpoint executes an impactful server-side state mutation (e.g., password change, email update, financial transaction, API key generation).
conditions.how_to_test: Does submitting the request alter database state, change account credentials, or trigger an external side effect?

conditions.condition: The target application relies on ambient credentials (session cookies, Basic auth, or TLS client certificates) for authorization.
conditions.how_to_test: Can the request be authorized using only automatically transmitted headers, without requiring an explicit Bearer token in the Authorization header?

conditions.condition: The request does not require or validate an unpredictable, unforgeable value (anti-CSRF token).
conditions.how_to_test: Can the request succeed when the anti-CSRF token parameter is omitted, submitted empty, or replaced with an arbitrary value?

conditions.condition: The session cookie explicitly declares 'SameSite=None', allowing cross-site form POST and subresource requests.
conditions.how_to_test: Inspect the Set-Cookie response header in browser developer tools: does it contain 'SameSite=None'?

conditions.condition: The state-changing endpoint accepts HTTP GET requests (or supports HTTP method switching from POST to GET), permitting exploitation via top-level navigations under SameSite=Lax.
conditions.how_to_test: Convert the POST request to a GET request with query parameters: does the server execute the state change?

conditions.condition: The client environment is a legacy browser (lacking Lax-by-default) OR the request exploits the Chromium 2-minute Lax-allowing-unsafe POST window.
conditions.how_to_test: Does the request succeed in target client environments lacking modern SameSite defaults or within 120 seconds of user login?

conditions.condition: The attacker controls a sibling subdomain or uses same-site contexts (e.g. *.example.com) to issue requests or manipulate cookies.
conditions.how_to_test: Can an attacker host content on a same-site subdomain (e.g. user-content.example.com) that bypasses SameSite=Lax boundaries?

exploitability.gate_rule: Every AND condition must evaluate to true. In the final group, at least one of the OR conditions must evaluate to true for the endpoint to be exploitable.

attack_surface: Account setting update endpoints (email change, password reset, 2FA toggle, phone number update)
Financial or transactional endpoints (funds transfer, invoice generation, checkout submission)
Administrative functionality (user creation, role modification, system configuration changes)
Social and messaging features (posting messages, sending invites, following accounts)
WebSocket handshake endpoints (HTTP 101 Upgrade requests for interactive full-duplex sockets)
Login / Logout endpoints (Login CSRF to trap victims in attacker accounts, Logout CSRF to cause denial of service)

hypotheses.hypothesis: The endpoint requires a valid anti-CSRF token and strictly validates it against the active server-side session.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Omitting or modifying the anti-CSRF token results in an immediate 403 Forbidden or 400 Bad Request error.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The endpoint validates the token only when present; omitting the token parameter entirely bypasses validation.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Submitting the form with the csrf_token field removed succeeds with 200 OK and applies the state mutation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The endpoint only validates the token on POST requests; switching to GET bypasses token checking.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Sending a GET request to the endpoint URL with query parameters executes the mutation without requiring a token.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The application relies entirely on SameSite=Lax cookies for CSRF protection and does not use tokens.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Cross-site POST requests fail because cookies are withheld, but top-level GET navigations carry cookies and succeed if the action accepts GET.

minimal_experiments.experiment: Intercept a legitimate state-changing request using an HTTP proxy. Remove the anti-CSRF token parameter from the request body entirely, while keeping the user's session cookie intact. Submit the modified request.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: Server returns 200/302 and state is modified → Token validation flaw confirmed (H2).
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: Server rejects request with 400/403/CSRF error → Token is mandatory; test method switching or session binding.
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Determines whether token validation is strictly enforced or merely optional in the request handler.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If blocked, test HTTP method switching (POST -> GET).

minimal_experiments.hypothesis: The application allows HTTP method switching (H3)
minimal_experiments.experiment: Send an HTTP GET request to the target endpoint with parameters moved to the URL query string (e.g. GET /settings/email?email=test@example.com).
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: Server processes the GET request and commits the state mutation → Vulnerable to top-level navigation CSRF (H3).
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: Server responds with 405 Method Not Allowed or refuses mutation → Endpoint requires POST.
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Identifies whether the endpoint is exploitable via top-level navigations under SameSite=Lax.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If method switching is prevented, inspect cookie SameSite flags and test for token session-binding flaws.

minimal_experiments.hypothesis: The token is not tied to the active user session
minimal_experiments.experiment: Generate a valid anti-CSRF token using Account A. Copy that token and submit it in a state-changing request authenticated with Account B's session cookie.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: Request succeeds → Application validates token existence globally but does not tie tokens to specific user sessions.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: Request rejected → Token is correctly bound to the authenticated user session.
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Proves whether an attacker can harvest their own valid CSRF token to attack other victims.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If bound, verify whether double-submit cookie patterns allow cookie tossing or subdomain injection.

decision_points.question: Does the request rely on ambient credentials (cookies/Basic auth) rather than explicit Bearer headers?
decision_points.no: Stop. Explicit Authorization headers cannot be forced across origins by the browser.

decision_points.question: Does the endpoint perform a state-changing action (write/update/delete)?
decision_points.no: Stop. Read-only endpoints are protected by the Same-Origin Policy from cross-origin data exposure.

decision_points.question: Is an anti-CSRF token required and strictly validated against the active session?
decision_points.yes: Investigate potential token bypasses (omission, method switching, cross-session reuse, duplicate cookie injection).
decision_points.no: Vulnerable to request forgery if cross-origin transport is possible.

decision_points.question: Does the cookie policy permit credential transmission (SameSite=None, state-changing GET, or 2-minute Lax window)?
decision_points.no: Mitigated by modern browser SameSite policy unless top-level navigation or sibling domain bypass exists.

what_must_be_proven: The state-changing request can be triggered from an external, untrusted origin.
The victim's browser automatically attaches valid ambient session credentials to the forged request.
The server processes the request and executes the state change without user interaction or approval.
The attacker does not need to know or predict unguessable tokens.

evidence.evidence: A proof-of-concept HTML page hosted on an external domain successfully changes the email or password of a logged-in test user upon visiting the page.
Differential proxy logs demonstrating that the endpoint processes state mutations when the CSRF token parameter is omitted or swapped with a different user's token.
Response headers confirm session cookies lack SameSite attributes or use SameSite=None, and HTML forms lack hidden CSRF token inputs.

confirmation.safe_confirmation: Construct an external HTML proof-of-concept form on a local web server (http://localhost:8080 or a private test domain). Target a harmless state change (e.g., updating a user bio or screen name) on a dedicated test account. Verify that loading the external page in a browser where the test account is logged in updates the bio without manual form interaction.

failed_attempts.attempt: Submitting a cross-origin XMLHttpRequest or fetch() with JSON body (Content-Type: application/json)
failed_attempts.result: Browser blocks the request with a CORS error before reaching the application logic.
failed_attempts.why: Requests with Content-Type: application/json are not 'simple requests' under CORS; the browser automatically issues an OPTIONS preflight request. If the server does not return permissive Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, the browser aborts the actual request.
failed_attempts.lesson: Classic CSRF requires simple request content types (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, text/plain) unless CORS is misconfigured or WebSockets are used.

failed_attempts.attempt: Auto-submitting a standard POST form against a modern browser with default SameSite=Lax
failed_attempts.result: Request arrives at the server without session cookies; server responds with 401 Unauthorized.
failed_attempts.why: Modern browsers withhold default Lax cookies on cross-site form POST requests.
failed_attempts.lesson: Do not assume modern browsers behave like legacy HTTP clients. Verify whether SameSite=None is set, test method switching to GET, or inspect the 120-second Lax-allowing-unsafe window.

capability_and_impact.primitive: Cross-origin HTTP request dispatch carrying ambient session credentials

capabilities.impact: Confirms ambient authority transport is active

capabilities.additional_prerequisite: Endpoint lacks effective anti-CSRF token validation
capabilities.impact: Low: Modification of non-sensitive preferences or profile metadata

capabilities.additional_prerequisite: Endpoint does not require current password confirmation or step-up authentication
capabilities.impact: Critical: Full account takeover by triggering password recovery to attacker's email

capabilities.additional_prerequisite: Banking or payment endpoint lacks secondary authorization (OTP/PIN/token)
