Whether the target application requires re-authentication (current password) for critical changes
Whether the application sends an out-of-band confirmation (email link) before finalizing state changes
Whether the session cookie uses SameSite=Strict, SameSite=Lax, or SameSite=None
Whether the browser environment is a modern desktop browser or an embedded mobile WebView

variants.name: Form-Based POST CSRF
variants.condition: The target endpoint expects a standard HTML form POST submission (application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data) and cookies are sent cross-site (SameSite=None or legacy browser).
variants.mechanism_detail: The attacker creates a hidden HTML <form> on their website with input fields pre-populated with attack values. JavaScript automatically submits the form via document.forms[0].submit() when the victim loads the page.
variants.investigation_difference: Test whether the endpoint processes standard form submissions without anti-CSRF tokens and whether cookies carry SameSite=None.
variants.how_to_identify: Inspect the legitimate form in browser dev tools: check if hidden input fields containing random tokens are absent or static.
variants.how_to_confirm: Create a local HTML page with the form and verify that loading the page mutates test account state.

variants.name: State-Changing GET CSRF
variants.condition: The application executes a state-changing operation via HTTP GET, or accepts GET requests interchangeably with POST.
variants.mechanism_detail: Because browsers treat top-level GET navigations as safe, SameSite=Lax cookies ARE attached. An attacker can trigger the action via a simple ,
variants.investigation_difference: Must test whether sensitive actions can be invoked via GET query parameters.
variants.how_to_identify: Submit the action using GET in an intercepting proxy. If the state changes on the server, the endpoint is vulnerable to GET CSRF.
variants.how_to_confirm: Place an tag pointing to the target URL on an external page and verify whether visiting the page triggers the state change.

variants.name: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH)
variants.condition: A WebSocket endpoint relies on ambient session cookies during the initial HTTP 101 Upgrade handshake without validating the Origin header.
variants.mechanism_detail: The attacker's site opens a new WebSocket connection to wss://target.com/ws. The browser includes session cookies in the handshake. Once connected, the attacker has a full-duplex, bidirectional communication channel capable of both writing commands and reading real-time responses.
variants.investigation_difference: Assess WebSocket handshake behavior: check if Origin header validation is enforced and whether SameSite=None is set on cookies.
variants.how_to_identify: Inspect the WebSocket connection in browser network tools; verify if the Upgrade request uses cookies and lacks origin-bound tokens.
variants.how_to_confirm: Use a client script on an external domain to connect to the socket and observe if onopen fires successfully.

variants.name: Login CSRF
variants.condition: The login form lacks anti-CSRF protection, allowing an attacker to force the victim's browser to log into the attacker's account.
variants.mechanism_detail: The attacker crafts a form that logs the victim into the attacker's account. When the victim subsequently enters sensitive data (such as credit card details, search history, or personal documents), the data is stored in the attacker's account for later retrieval.
variants.investigation_difference: Focuses on unauthenticated login endpoints rather than authenticated account settings.
variants.how_to_identify: Check whether the login form includes a CSRF token and whether login sessions can be established cross-origin.
variants.how_to_confirm: Verify that a cross-origin form submission switches the active browser session to a predetermined attacker account.

defense_analysis.assumption: The token is cryptographically random, tied to the user's active session, and cannot be read by an external origin under the Same-Origin Policy.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The token must be generated using a CSPRNG, stored server-side in the session or validated cryptographically, required on all mutating requests, and never exposed in URLs (which leak in Referer headers) or cross-origin scripts.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Tokens are omitted from validation on HTTP method switch; tokens are not validated when omitted; tokens are pooled globally and not bound to the submitting user's session; or XSS allows the attacker to read the token directly from the DOM.
defense_analysis.investigation: Test token edge cases: omit the token, send an empty token, send an invalid token, or send a valid token from a different user session.

defense_analysis.assumption: The browser enforces RFC 6265bis and withholds session cookies on cross-site dispatches.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The user must be using a modern browser; the application must not perform state changes via GET (for Lax); and no sibling subdomains or 2-minute Lax windows can be abused.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Sensitive actions accept GET requests (exploitable via Lax top-level navigation); or the application explicitly configures SameSite=None for cross-domain functionality.
defense_analysis.investigation: Inspect the Set-Cookie headers for SameSite values and test if state-changing endpoints accept GET requests.

defense_analysis.assumption: The server inspects Sec-Fetch-Site and rejects requests where the value is 'cross-site' for state-changing routes.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: Browser must support Fetch Metadata; backend middleware must consistently inspect the header before dispatching to business logic.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Middleware allows cross-site requests if Sec-Fetch-Site is missing (legacy clients) or fails to apply rules to specific API subpaths.
defense_analysis.investigation: Strip or manipulate the Sec-Fetch-Site header in an intercepting proxy to test fallback behavior.

defense_analysis.assumption: Browsers cannot send custom headers cross-origin without triggering a CORS preflight that the target server denies.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The server must strictly require the header and verify its presence; CORS must not allow arbitrary origins.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Server treats the header as optional; or CORS misconfiguration returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials.
defense_analysis.investigation: Submit the request without the custom header to check if the server processes the payload.

defense_analysis.assumption: The server sets a random value in both a cookie and a request parameter (hidden form field or custom header). On submission, the server compares the cookie value against the parameter value. An attacker cannot read the cookie value cross-origin under the Same-Origin Policy, so they cannot include the matching parameter.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The cookie must use the __Host- prefix (preventing domain-scoped overrides); no sibling subdomain can inject or overwrite cookies via cookie tossing; the comparison must be timing-safe; and the cookie value must be cryptographically random and tied to the user session.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: An attacker controlling a sibling subdomain (e.g., user-content.example.com) can set a domain-scoped cookie for .example.com, overwriting the CSRF cookie with a known value. The attacker then submits the matching known value in the form parameter. Without the __Host- prefix, MITM attackers on HTTP subdomains can also inject cookies. If the CSRF cookie is not tied to the session, an attacker can use their own valid cookie-parameter pair.
defense_analysis.investigation: Check whether the CSRF cookie uses __Host- prefix. Test if a cookie set from a sibling subdomain overwrites the CSRF cookie. Verify whether submitting a self-generated cookie-parameter pair from a different session succeeds.

defense_analysis.assumption: The server inspects the Origin or Referer request header to verify that the request was initiated from the same origin, rejecting cross-origin submissions.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: The browser must always send the Origin header on state-changing requests; the server must reject requests when Origin is absent or does not match the expected value; Referer must not be suppressed by Referrer-Policy.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: The Origin header may be omitted on certain cross-origin redirects or by privacy-focused browser extensions. The Referer header can be suppressed entirely by setting Referrer-Policy: no-referrer on the attacker's page. Some server implementations fall back to allowing the request when Origin is missing (null or absent), which can be triggered by sandboxed iframes (e.g., <iframe sandbox='allow-forms'>).
defense_analysis.investigation: Submit the state-changing request with the Origin header removed or set to 'null'. Test with Referer suppressed via Referrer-Policy. Check if the server accepts requests when both headers are absent.

common_misconceptions.why_wrong: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie via document.cookie (defending against XSS-based token theft). It does NOT prevent the browser from automatically attaching the cookie to cross-origin HTTP requests. CSRF exploits the browser's automatic cookie attachment, not JavaScript cookie access.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: HttpOnly is an XSS defense, not a CSRF defense. CSRF is mitigated by anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and Fetch Metadata — mechanisms that verify request provenance, not cookie readability.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Using POST instead of GET prevents CSRF.
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: HTML <form method='POST'> elements can be auto-submitted cross-origin via JavaScript (document.forms[0].submit()). The browser dispatches the POST request and attaches cookies exactly as it would for a same-origin form. POST is not a security boundary.
common_misconceptions.correct_model:
POST prevents CSRF via or tags (which only dispatch GET), but not via
or fetch(). The actual defense is an unpredictable token or SameSite cookie policy, not the HTTP method.

common_misconceptions.why_wrong: CORS controls whether the browser allows JavaScript to read cross-origin responses. It does NOT prevent the browser from sending the cross-origin request in the first place. Standard HTML form submissions bypass CORS entirely — no preflight is issued. The state-changing request reaches the server and executes before any CORS response check.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: CORS is a read-access control, not a write-access control. CSRF exploits cross-origin writing (which CORS does not restrict for simple requests). Misconfigured CORS actually makes CSRF worse by allowing the attacker to also read responses.

common_misconceptions.misconception: SameSite=Lax means CSRF is dead and no longer requires defensive engineering.
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: SameSite=Lax attaches cookies on top-level GET navigations. Any application endpoint that performs state changes on GET (or accepts GET interchangeably with POST via method override) remains fully exploitable. Additionally, the Chromium 2-minute Lax-allowing-unsafe window permits cross-site POST within 120 seconds of cookie creation. Mobile WebViews and legacy embedded browsers may not enforce Lax-by-default.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: SameSite=Lax is a significant mitigation layer, not a complete solution. Applications must still enforce anti-CSRF tokens on state-changing endpoints, must never perform mutations on GET, and must account for non-standard client environments.

common_misconceptions.misconception: CSRF only affects forms — APIs using JSON are immune.
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: While JSON Content-Type (application/json) triggers a CORS preflight that blocks the request if the server denies it, this defense relies on the server NOT returning permissive CORS headers. If CORS is misconfigured (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * or reflects the Origin header with credentials), JSON API endpoints are fully exploitable. Additionally, some frameworks accept form-encoded bodies on JSON endpoints via content negotiation.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: JSON APIs are protected by the CORS preflight mechanism only if CORS is correctly configured. The actual defense is the same: validate anti-CSRF tokens or enforce strict origin checking.

false_positives.observation: The HTML form does not contain a visible anti-CSRF token hidden field.
false_positives.incorrect_conclusion: The endpoint is vulnerable to CSRF.
false_positives.why_incorrect: The anti-CSRF token may be transmitted via a custom HTTP header (e.g., X-CSRF-Token) set by JavaScript rather than a hidden form field. Single-page applications commonly use this pattern, attaching the token from meta tags or cookies via fetch() headers.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Inspect the actual XHR/fetch request in browser developer tools. Check if a custom header carries the token. Test whether the endpoint rejects requests without the header.

false_positives.observation: A cross-origin form submission reaches the server and returns a 200 OK response.
false_positives.incorrect_conclusion: CSRF is confirmed — the state change executed.
false_positives.why_incorrect: The server may have processed the request but rejected the state mutation internally, returning 200 OK with an error message in the response body (e.g., 'Invalid CSRF token' in a JSON response). Some frameworks return 200 with error payloads rather than 403.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Verify that the server-side state actually changed (e.g., check if the email was updated in the database or the transfer was committed). Do not rely solely on HTTP status codes.

false_positives.observation: The session cookie has SameSite=None configured.
false_positives.incorrect_conclusion: All endpoints on the application are vulnerable to CSRF.
false_positives.why_incorrect: The application may still enforce anti-CSRF tokens, Fetch Metadata validation, or custom header requirements on state-changing endpoints. SameSite=None removes one defense layer but does not eliminate all others.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Test whether state-changing requests succeed when anti-CSRF tokens are omitted, invalid, or from a different session.

failed_attempts.attempt: Submit a cross-origin fetch() request with Content-Type: application/json to a JSON API endpoint.
failed_attempts.result: Browser issues an OPTIONS preflight request. Server denies the preflight (no Access-Control-Allow-Origin). Browser aborts the actual request.
failed_attempts.why: Requests with Content-Type: application/json are not 'simple requests' under CORS. The browser automatically sends a preflight OPTIONS request. Unless the server returns permissive CORS headers, the actual request is never dispatched.
failed_attempts.lesson: Classic CSRF requires 'simple' content types (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, text/plain) unless CORS is misconfigured. For JSON APIs, verify CORS configuration before assuming immunity.

failed_attempts.attempt: Auto-submit a hidden POST form targeting a modern application with default SameSite=Lax cookies.
failed_attempts.result: Request arrives at the server without session cookies. Server returns 401 Unauthorized.
failed_attempts.why: Modern browsers withhold Lax cookies on cross-site subresource requests, including form POST submissions. The cookie is only attached on top-level navigations using safe HTTP methods (GET, HEAD).
failed_attempts.lesson: Do not assume all browsers behave like legacy HTTP clients. Verify whether SameSite=None is explicitly set, whether method switching to GET is possible, or whether the 2-minute Lax-allowing-unsafe window applies.

failed_attempts.attempt: Use an tag to trigger a state-changing GET request under SameSite=Lax.
failed_attempts.result: Browser sends the GET request but withholds the Lax session cookie.
failed_attempts.why: An tag load is a subresource request, not a top-level navigation. SameSite=Lax only attaches cookies to top-level navigations (address bar changes). Subresource requests are treated the same as SameSite=Strict for Lax cookies.
failed_attempts.lesson: For state-changing GET CSRF under SameSite=Lax, the request must be a top-level navigation (<a> click, window.location redirect, or <meta http-equiv='refresh'>), not a subresource load.

transfer.shared_mechanism: Origin-Context Confusion: an untrusted origin coerces a client runtime with ambient credentials into issuing unauthorized instructions to a trusting server sink.

related_topics.shared_principle: CORS controls cross-origin reading; CSRF exploits cross-origin writing. Misconfigured CORS (e.g. Access-Control-Allow-Origin with credentials) enables full cross-origin CSRF with response readability.
Both exploit the authenticated user's session via an attacker-controlled page. Clickjacking tricks the user into physically clicking the authentic UI, bypassing anti-CSRF tokens.
XSS executes inside the trusted origin, allowing the attacker to read anti-CSRF tokens directly from the DOM, completely defeating CSRF protections.

transfer.transferable_reasoning: Look for any architecture where: (1) an action performs a state mutation, (2) the server relies on ambient credentials (cookies, client certs, basic auth) to authorize the caller, and (3) the initiation context is not cryptographically validated. This reasoning applies across WebSockets, GraphQL mutations, embedded widgets, and internal web portals.
new_contexts: WebSocket handshakes (CSWSH) establishing full-duplex authenticated connections
GraphQL mutation endpoints using cookie-based authentication
Internal router or IoT administration web interfaces accessible via intranet IP
SaaS webhook integrations triggered via browser navigation
OAuth 2.0 authorization endpoints lacking state parameter validation (OAuth Login CSRF)
Mobile native apps handling custom URI schemes from web pages

sources.title: W3C - Fetch Metadata Request Headers
sources.claim: Defines Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, and Sec-Fetch-Dest headers enabling servers to enforce origin isolation policies deterministically.

sources.title: Chromium - SameSite Cookie Changes Projects
sources.claim: Documents the implementation of SameSite=Lax by default and the 2-minute Lax-allowing-unsafe exception for top-level POST requests.

claims.statement: The Same-Origin Policy (RFC 6454) restricts cross-origin reading of response data via DOM and XMLHttpRequest/Fetch, but does not block cross-origin writing/sending of requests (such as HTML form submissions, image loads, or script tags), allowing an untrusted origin to dispatch requests to a target application.
claims.scope: All standard web browsers implementing the W3C / WHATWG Same-Origin Policy

claims.statement: Browsers automatically attach matching ambient credentials (HTTP cookies, cached HTTP authentication headers, TLS client certificates) to outbound HTTP requests based solely on the target domain, without verifying whether the request was intentionally triggered by the user within the authentic application context.
claims.scope: Default browser HTTP client behavior for requests matching domain and path scoping rules (subject to SameSite constraints)

claims.statement: Per RFC 6265bis, SameSite=Lax cookies are withheld on cross-site subresource requests (e.g. cross-origin form POSTs, fetch/XHR, ), but are automatically attached to top-level navigations that use safe HTTP methods (GET and HEAD), leaving state-changing GET endpoints vulnerable to cross-site exploitation.
claims.scope: Browsers implementing RFC 6265bis SameSite cookie semantics

claims.statement: Anti-CSRF synchronizer tokens protect state-changing endpoints because they are origin-bound and cryptographically unpredictable; under the Same-Origin Policy, an external attacker origin cannot read the token from the victim's DOM or response headers.
claims.scope: Web applications using cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators (CSPRNG) tied to the user's active session and validated on all mutating requests

claims.statement: Fetch Metadata request headers (Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site) allow servers to deterministically identify and reject cross-origin request initiation before executing application business logic, neutralizing both GET- and POST-based CSRF without per-form token tracking.
claims.scope: Modern browsers supporting W3C Fetch Metadata Request Headers

claims.statement: The WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) performs an HTTP Upgrade handshake that includes the browser's ambient session cookies and an 'Origin' header, but is not restricted by the Same-Origin Policy; unless the server explicitly validates the Origin header during handshake negotiation, a cross-site attacker can establish a full-duplex authenticated socket session.
claims.scope: WebSocket servers relying on cookie-based authentication without origin validation

claims.statement: Chromium-based browsers implement a temporary 'Lax-allowing-unsafe' compatibility window where cookies that lack an explicit SameSite attribute are sent on cross-site top-level POST requests if the cookie was set (created or updated via a new Set-Cookie header) within the preceding 120 seconds. Session rotation or re-authentication that issues a fresh Set-Cookie header re-opens this window.
claims.scope: Chromium browsers (Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera) running the default SameSite transition policy

learning_objectives.observable_action: Given an authenticated state-changing feature, analyze its transport and authentication mechanisms to determine whether ambient credentials (cookies) are vulnerable to cross-site dispatch.
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Learner correctly identifies the credential transmission behavior across SameSite=Strict, Lax, and None policies, distinguishing subresource dispatches from top-level navigations.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Evaluate application-layer anti-CSRF defenses (synchronizer tokens, double-submit cookies, custom headers) and determine whether underlying assumptions are violated (e.g. token omitted on method switch, token not tied to session, predictable PRNG).

learning_objectives.observable_action: Apply the invariant of Origin-Context Confusion to non-traditional web contexts (such as WebSocket handshakes, GraphQL endpoints, or API gateways) and design minimal safe verification experiments.

prompt.setup: A financial brokerage platform provides a real-time order execution terminal at https://trade.apex-markets.com/terminal. When an authenticated trader loads the page, client-side JavaScript establishes a WebSocket connection to wss://trade.apex-markets.com/ws/orders. The browser attaches the trader's ambient session cookie (session_id) during the initial HTTP 101 Switching Protocols upgrade request. The session cookie is configured as 'SameSite=None; Secure' because the firm previously embedded chart widgets on affiliate marketing domains. Once connected, the WebSocket channel accepts JSON-formatted trading instructions (e.g., {"action":"SUBMIT_ORDER","pair":"ETH/USD","side":"BUY","amount":5.0}). No secondary unpredictable value is passed in the WebSocket handshake query parameters or initial frame to prove the request originated from the real terminal page, and the server application does not inspect the HTTP Origin header.
prompt.task_question: Analyze this architecture: (1) Formulate the security invariant and explain why the Same-Origin Policy does not prevent an external web page from opening this socket. (2) Map the trust boundary transition and ambient credential flow. (3) Formulate three mutually exclusive hypotheses regarding handshake validation. (4) Propose a minimal safe experiment to test exploitability without triggering unauthorized financial trades.

expected_reasoning.invariant_analysis: The security invariant requires that state-changing operations and authenticated communication channels cannot be initiated without verifying that the request originated from the authentic application interface. The violation condition occurs because the server treats the presence of ambient session cookies during the WebSocket upgrade handshake as proof of authorized user intent, while the WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) permits cross-origin connections without enforcing the Same-Origin Policy.
expected_reasoning.boundary_analysis: The trust boundary is crossed during the HTTP 101 Upgrade request. An attacker page hosted on https://malicious-trader.com uses new WebSocket('wss://trade.apex-markets.com/ws/orders'). Because the cookie has SameSite=None, the victim's browser automatically attaches Cookie: session_id=XYZ. The target server completes the handshake, establishing a bidirectional, full-duplex communication channel directly between the attacker's script and the authenticated trading engine.
competing_hypotheses: Hypothesis A (Unvalidated Origin): The server does not inspect the Origin header or validate it against an allowlist, allowing cross-origin WebSocket establishment and subsequent bidirectional order manipulation.

Hypothesis B (Reverse Proxy Origin Filtering): An intermediate reverse proxy (e.g. Cloudflare, AWS ALB, NGINX) inspects the Origin header and drops or terminates upgrade handshakes where Origin != trade.apex-markets.com.

Hypothesis C (In-Frame Authentication Required): Although the HTTP handshake succeeds, the application layer requires an explicit authentication frame (e.g., an in-memory JWT or ephemeral token) before accepting trade commands.
expected_reasoning.minimal_safe_experiment: Host a static HTML page on an external test domain that executes new WebSocket('wss://trade.apex-markets.com/ws/orders'). Upon onopen, send a read-only or harmless diagnostic ping frame (e.g. {"action":"PING"} or {"action":"GET_SERVER_TIME"}) and log the onmessage event. Stop immediately if connection is established and server responds; under NO circumstances submit BUY/SELL order frames.
expected_reasoning.capability_calibration: The proven primitive is cross-origin full-duplex socket establishment with ambient session credentials. This is significantly more severe than standard CSRF: because WebSockets are bidirectional and not bound by SOP read restrictions once opened, the attacker gains both WRITE (submitting orders) and READ (reading streaming trade executions and portfolio balances) capabilities.
expected_reasoning.remaining_uncertainties: Whether the backend requires secondary trade confirmation signatures (e.g., 2FA/PIN); whether rate limiters disconnect unusual origin patterns; whether order frames require non-ambient transaction nonces.

scoring_rubric.description: Ability to identify the protected security guarantee and its violation condition across non-HTTP transport.

levels.0: Fails to identify any invariant; confuses CSRF with XSS or network eavesdropping.
levels.1: Mentions that WebSockets are insecure or that trading should be protected.
levels.2: Identifies that cross-origin scripts should not be able to connect to private endpoints.
levels.3: Explicitly articulates that establishing an authenticated socket channel must verify request origin provenance and user intentionality, not just cookie presence.
levels.4: Rigorously formulates the invariant and defines the exact violation condition in terms of RFC 6455 handshake ambient authority and Origin header neglect.

scoring_rubric.description: Accuracy in mapping untrusted cross-origin input through the browser confused deputy to the target WebSocket engine.

levels.0: Does not understand how WebSockets connect or assumes SOP blocks cross-origin sockets.
levels.1: Recognizes browser connects to the server but confuses client-side cookies with server-side tokens.
levels.2: Traces that evil.com initiates the connection and the browser includes cookies because of SameSite=None.
levels.3: Accurately maps the full boundary: external origin -> browser WebSocket API -> HTTP 101 Upgrade with ambient cookies -> target server handshake sink.
levels.4: Traces the complete boundary crossing, contrasting SOP read restrictions in HTTP with the bidirectional read/write capabilities unlocked by cross-site WebSocket establishment.

scoring_rubric.description: Formulation of falsifiable, mutually exclusive competing hypotheses regarding server handshake handling.

levels.0: No hypotheses formulated; assumes immediate total financial theft without testing.
levels.1: Single hypothesis stating that the platform is vulnerable to CSRF.
levels.2: Proposes two vague hypotheses without clear demarcation of protocol vs application layers.
levels.3: Formulates distinct hypotheses distinguishing between missing Origin header checks, proxy-layer filtering, and application-layer frame authentication.
levels.4: Proposes a comprehensive, mutually exclusive set of hypotheses isolating transport upgrade, origin inspection, and subsequent socket message authorization.

scoring_rubric.description: Selection of minimal, non-destructive experiments producing maximum information gain without financial harm.

levels.0: Proposes sending BUY/SELL market orders or spamming orders to see what executes.
levels.1: Proposes copying an exploit script from GitHub without modifying target payloads.
levels.2: Proposes connecting a socket but attempts a small trade ($1) to verify execution.
levels.3: Designs a non-destructive experiment: connects socket from test origin and observes onopen or sends harmless diagnostic ping.
levels.4: Designs a strictly non-destructive diagnostic experiment with explicit stop conditions, testing origin rejection without emitting state-mutating order frames.

scoring_rubric.description: Strict separation between the demonstrated connection primitive, bidirectional data flow, and hypothetical trade execution.

levels.0: Equates connecting a WebSocket with immediate total drainage of the user's bank account.
levels.1: Confuses standard blind CSRF (write-only) with CSWSH without realizing CSWSH enables reading responses.
levels.2: Identifies that messages can be sent, but does not distinguish between connection success and order validation.
levels.3: Accurately calibrates that successful handshake provides a bidirectional channel, but trading impact remains subject to frame-level validations.
levels.4: Rigorously separates the primitive (cross-origin authenticated WebSocket handshake) from capabilities (bidirectional frame I/O, event eavesdropping) and business impact (unauthorized trade execution).

scoring_rubric.description: Identification of unknown architectural factors that require further validation before reaching definitive conclusions.

levels.0: Expresses complete certainty without empirical observation.
levels.1: Vaguely acknowledges that something might not work.
levels.2: Mentions that there might be a firewall or antivirus blocking the connection.
levels.3: Explicitly details key technical unknowns: Origin header filtering at reverse proxy, in-frame token requirements, and secondary trade confirmation.
levels.4: Formulates an exhaustive matrix of open uncertainties with corresponding diagnostic probes for each architectural layer.

common_learner_errors.error: Assuming the Same-Origin Policy blocks cross-origin WebSocket connections
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: RFC 6455 deliberately allows cross-origin WebSocket connections; browsers do not apply SOP to WebSockets. Instead, browsers send an Origin header and leave it to the server to accept or reject the handshake.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Review concept.same-origin-policy and RFC 6455 §1.3 to understand how transport protocols differ in cross-origin boundaries.

common_learner_errors.error: Submitting a live trade order payload to confirm the vulnerability during an assessment
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: Executing a state-changing transaction violates ethical boundaries and engagement scope, potentially causing real financial loss or legal liability.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Always use harmless diagnostic frames (PING or non-mutating query) to verify authenticated socket communication.

common_learner_errors.error: Believing HttpOnly cookies prevent Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading cookies via document.cookie. The browser automatically attaches HttpOnly cookies to the HTTP Upgrade handshake header regardless.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Study concept.ambient-credentials to understand that HttpOnly is an XSS defense, not a CSRF or CSWSH defense.

scenarios.title: Account Email Update with Inconsistent Server-Side Validation

prompt.setup: A SaaS collaboration platform allows users to change their account email address at POST /api/user/email. The form in the UI includes a hidden, random value generated server-side and embedded as a form field. The session cookie is configured as 'SameSite=None; Secure'. During initial testing, you observe that submitting the form with this value altered or removed returns 403 Forbidden. However, you notice that the API endpoint is written using a generic web framework request handler.
prompt.task_question: Analyze this endpoint: (1) Formulate three hypotheses regarding how the server validates this hidden value. (2) Propose safe differential experiments to verify whether that validation can be bypassed.

expected_reasoning.invariant_analysis: The invariant requires that the server strictly validates a valid, session-tied anti-CSRF token on every state-changing request.
expected_reasoning.boundary_analysis: Attacker origin crafts a cross-origin request targeting /api/user/email, testing if validation assumptions can be broken.
competing_hypotheses: Hypothesis 1 (Token Omission): The server only validates the token IF the token parameter is present in the request; omitting the parameter entirely bypasses validation.

Hypothesis 2 (Method Switching): The server only enforces token validation on POST requests; switching the HTTP method to GET (e.g. /api/user/email?email=attacker@evil.com) causes the backend to execute the state change without checking the token.

Hypothesis 3 (Session Disconnect): The server validates that the token is cryptographically valid in its global token pool, but does not verify that the token belongs to the specific user session submitting the request.
expected_reasoning.minimal_safe_experiment: Using an authorized test account, issue safe differential requests: (a) submit a POST with the csrf_token parameter removed, changing the email to an alias of the tester (test+safe@tester.com); (b) submit a GET request with the same parameter; (c) submit a POST with a token generated by a secondary tester account.
expected_reasoning.capability_calibration: Demonstrating token omission or method switching confirms full form-based CSRF leading to complete account takeover via password reset redirection.
expected_reasoning.remaining_uncertainties: Whether the application sends an email verification link to the old address before committing the change.

scoring_rubric.description: Formulation of the token validation invariant.

levels.0: Fails to identify the invariant.
levels.1: Mentions that CSRF tokens are present.
levels.2: Identifies that tokens must prevent unauthorized form submissions.
levels.3: Explains that the token must be origin-bound, unpredictable, and strictly tied to the active session.
levels.4: Rigorously defines the mathematical and session-binding guarantees required of the token validation logic.

scoring_rubric.description: Mapping the parameter validation layer vs application sink.

levels.0: Does not map request parameters.
levels.1: Notes that the token is sent in the body.
levels.2: Maps the token from client form to server validation filter.
levels.3: Traces boundary between framework middleware (token check) and application route handler.
levels.4: Thoroughly maps framework routing, method dispatching, and session-token binding.

scoring_rubric.description: Formulation of token validation bypass hypotheses.

levels.0: No hypotheses formulated.
levels.1: Hypothesizes guessing the token.
levels.2: Proposes one bypass idea (e.g. remove token).
levels.3: Proposes distinct hypotheses: omission, method switching, and session mismatch.
levels.4: Systematic hypothesis matrix covering omission, method toggle, duplicate token, and cross-session reuse.

scoring_rubric.description: Designing safe differential tests.

levels.0: Attempts destructive actions against live users.
levels.1: Uses automated scanner without calibration.
levels.2: Changes test account email to arbitrary address.
levels.3: Uses controlled tester email alias to observe behavior safely.
levels.4: Designs paired differential experiments isolating each token validation condition with controlled rollbacks.

scoring_rubric.description: Separation of token bypass from account takeover.

levels.0: Equates finding a parameter with full RCE.
levels.1: Assumes email change instantly yields account takeover without checking confirmation emails.
levels.2: Notes email is updated.
levels.3: Calibrates that email change enables account recovery hijack if no confirmation loop exists.
levels.4: Precisely bounds the attack chain from token validation defect to account takeover prerequisites.

scoring_rubric.description: Identifying application logic confirmation steps.

levels.0: Assumes zero uncertainties.
levels.1: Vaguely wonders if it worked.
levels.2: Notes confirmation email might be sent.
levels.3: Documents key uncertainties: confirmation tokens to old email, re-auth prompt, session invalidation.
levels.4: Comprehensive audit matrix of post-mutation lifecycle uncertainties.

common_learner_errors.error: Assuming the presence of a CSRF token parameter in HTML proves the endpoint is secure
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: Many applications render a token field in the HTML form but fail to validate it on the backend, or skip validation when the parameter is omitted or HTTP method is changed to GET.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Always perform differential testing: verify that requests FAIL when the token is missing, invalid, or tied to another session.

common_learner_errors.error: Testing CSRF token bypass using an attacker's email on an executive or production user account
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: Overwriting another user's email disrupts business operations and violates testing scope.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Always conduct CSRF verification between two dedicated test accounts under your own control.
