aliases: web cache poisoning via host header
learning_objectives: Given an HTTP request/response pair, determine whether the Host header (or a forwarding header such as X-Forwarded-Host) is reflected into a generated absolute URL, a cache key, or a routing decision.
Given a password-reset or email-notification flow, design a minimal experiment using header manipulation to determine whether the generated link's domain is attacker-controllable.
Distinguish routing-based Host trust (virtual host dispatch) from output-based Host trust (URL generation, cache keying) as distinct exploitation surfaces that share one underlying mechanism.

Given a defense that validates the Host header against an allowlist, identify whether a sibling header (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Server) is read by the same code path without the same validation.

safety_contract.authorization_assumption: Testing occurs only against a target with explicit written authorization to modify Host, X-Forwarded-Host, and X-Forwarded-Server headers, and to trigger password-reset or notification flows.
scope_constraints: Do not trigger password-reset or notification flows for real user accounts outside an authorized test account.
Do not deliver crafted links to real third parties outside the authorized test scope.
Confine cache-poisoning experiments to isolated test paths that will not be served to live traffic.
stop_conditions: Stop immediately if a reset token or session identifier belonging to a real, non-test user appears in a collaborator server's logs.
Stop if a cache-poisoning experiment begins affecting responses served to unrelated live traffic rather than an isolated test resource.
safety_contract.safer_alternative: Use a test account you control and an intercepting proxy (e.g. Burp Repeater) rather than triggering flows against arbitrary usernames; use a collaborator/exploit-server domain you own to observe whether the server embeds it, rather than a domain belonging to someone else.

applies_when: The application dynamically builds an absolute URL (email links, canonical link headers, redirect targets, OAuth metadata) from the Host header, X-Forwarded-Host, or X-Forwarded-Server instead of a fixed, server-configured domain.
The web server or framework uses the Host header to select a virtual host, routing rule, or cache key.
A caching layer sits in front of the origin and its cache-key computation omits a header that the origin's response actually varies on.
does_not_apply_when: The origin derives its canonical domain from fixed server-side configuration and never consults the Host header for anything security-relevant.
The request-target is sent in absolute-form and the origin correctly prioritizes it over the Host header per RFC 9112, with no later fallback path that re-reads the header.
An edge proxy enforces a strict Host allowlist and rejects or rewrites mismatched Host headers before the request reaches application logic that generates URLs or routes on it.
variance_notes: Django's get_host() historically mishandled userinfo-style syntax in the Host header (e.g. 'validsite.com:random@evilsite.com'), allowing an attacker-chosen domain into password-reset link generation before this was patched at the framework level.

Some deployments trust X-Forwarded-Host or X-Forwarded-Server from any client because they assume these headers are only ever set by a trusted upstream proxy — true only if the edge explicitly strips client-supplied values with those names before forwarding.

RFC 9112 requires an origin server to ignore the Host header when the request-target is in absolute-form; implementations that consult the Host header as a fallback after this precedence rule remain exploitable even in otherwise-compliant HTTP/1.1 stacks.

mental_model.one_sentence: Some applications treat the client-supplied Host header as if it were verified server identity, when it is really just another piece of attacker-controlled input.
mental_model.short_explanation: The Host header tells a server which website the client thinks it is reaching. Some applications use that same header to build absolute URLs (password-reset links), choose a cache key, or make a routing decision, without confirming it matches a server-configured, trusted value. Because the client fully controls this header, an attacker can substitute their own domain, and the server will faithfully embed that value into content or decisions that other trusting parties later act on.

analogy.text: It is like a hotel forwarding your mail to whatever return address you wrote on the envelope, instead of checking which room you are actually registered in.
analogy.where_it_breaks: The analogy breaks down because nothing is 'returned' to the attacker directly. The poisoned content is instead delivered to a separate victim or into a shared cache.

invariant.statement: A value supplied entirely by the client (Host, X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Server) must not be trusted as authoritative for generating security-sensitive output unless it has been validated against a server-controlled allowlist.
invariant.why_it_matters: Password-reset links, canonical URLs, and cache keys all assume the domain component reflects the application's real, intended origin. If that assumption is false, the server will unknowingly manufacture attacker-influenced content that other trusted parties treat as legitimate.
invariant.violation_condition: The Host header, or a forwarding header trusted in its place, is reflected unvalidated into a generated absolute URL, a routing decision, or a cache key, with no independent server-side check confirming it matches an expected value.
invariant.investigation_question: If I change the Host header, or a forwarding header, to a domain I control, does anything the server generates, routes, or caches change to reflect my value?

normal_behavior.description: The application either ignores the Host header entirely for anything security-sensitive, deriving its canonical domain from a fixed server-side configuration value, or validates the incoming Host header against a strict allowlist before using it for routing, caching, or URL generation. Requests bearing an unrecognized Host value are rejected or routed to a fixed default vhost that performs no sensitive URL generation.

vulnerable_behavior.description: The application reads the Host header, or a related X-Forwarded-* header, directly from the incoming request and threads it unchecked into an absolute URL that gets emailed, redirected to, or embedded as a canonical link — or uses it to key a shared cache or select a virtual host — without confirming it matches a server-configured expected value.

steps: The client sends an HTTP request specifying an arbitrary value in the Host header, or a forwarding header such as X-Forwarded-Host.
The origin server, or a component behind a reverse proxy, reads this header to determine 'which domain this request is for', for use in routing, cache keying, or URL construction.
Application logic uses this value to build an absolute URL or to select cache/routing behavior, without independently confirming it matches an expected, server-controlled domain.
The resulting content is delivered to a party other than the attacker: a victim's inbox, or any client requesting the same cached resource.

The victim's trust in the delivered content converts the attacker's chosen value into a security-relevant action: a password-reset token leaked to an attacker-controlled domain, or a poisoned page served to future visitors.

data_flow.source: Client-controlled HTTP request header: Host, X-Forwarded-Host, or X-Forwarded-Server.
transformations: Header value is read by the web server or application framework.
Value is concatenated or interpolated into an absolute URL string, or used directly as a cache-key or routing key.
data_flow.parser_or_component: The application framework's URL-generation helper, or the caching/routing layer that keys on the Host header.
data_flow.sink_or_decision: The generated URL is embedded in an outbound email or HTTP response, or a routing/caching decision is made based on the header value.
data_flow.result: An attacker-chosen domain is delivered to a third party as if it were the legitimate application domain, or a cache entry keyed incorrectly serves attacker-influenced content to other visitors.

trust_transformation.attacker_data: Client-supplied Host, X-Forwarded-Host, or X-Forwarded-Server header value.
trust_transformation.parser_or_interpreter: The application's URL-construction logic, or the caching/routing layer, which treats the header as equivalent to a server-verified domain.
trust_transformation.new_meaning: An arbitrary client-supplied string is reinterpreted as 'the trusted domain of this application.'
trust_transformation.authority_gained: The attacker gains the ability to make the server manufacture and distribute content that appears to originate from, and will be trusted as belonging to, the legitimate application.
trust_transformation.effect: Sensitive tokens embedded in that content can be redirected to an attacker-controlled domain, or poisoned content can be served from cache to unrelated future visitors.

conditions.condition: The Host header, or a forwarding header, is reflected into a security-relevant output: URL generation, a cache key, or a routing decision.
conditions.how_to_test: Change the Host header to a collaborator domain you control and observe whether it appears in a generated link, a cached response, or affects which content is served.

conditions.label: No independent validation blocks the untrusted value

conditions.condition: No server-side allowlist check confirms the Host value matches a known-good domain before it is used.
An allowlist check exists but validates only the 'Host' header, while the vulnerable code path actually reads a different header (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host) that bypasses the check.

exploitability.gate_rule: The reflection condition must hold, AND at least one path around validation must exist, for the attack to be exploitable.

attack_surface: Password-reset and account-verification email flows that embed a server-generated link
Canonical URL, Open Graph, or sitemap generation that echoes the request's Host
Reverse-proxied deployments where the origin trusts X-Forwarded-Host or X-Forwarded-Server from the client rather than from the proxy
Caching layers (CDN or reverse-proxy cache) whose cache key does not include a header the origin's response varies on
Virtual-host routing / SNI-independent dispatch based purely on the Host header

hypotheses.hypothesis: The application ignores the Host header entirely for URL generation and uses a fixed server-side domain.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Changing the Host header has no effect on any generated link or canonical URL.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The application reflects the raw Host header into generated URLs without validation.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Changing the Host header changes the domain in a generated password-reset or notification link.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The application validates 'Host' but a sibling forwarding header (X-Forwarded-Host) is read unvalidated by the same code path.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: Changing 'Host' alone has no effect, but adding X-Forwarded-Host with a collaborator domain changes the generated URL.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A caching layer, not the origin, is responsible for any observed effect, rather than the origin trusting the header for URL generation.
hypotheses.predicted_observation: The effect only appears on subsequent, cached responses to other requests, rather than in the direct response to the crafted request itself.

minimal_experiments.experiment: Trigger a password-reset (or similar link-generating) request for a test account you control, once with the normal Host header and once with a collaborator domain substituted in.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: The resulting email/notification link's domain matches your collaborator domain.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: The link's domain remains the application's real domain regardless of the Host header sent.
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Directly distinguishes whether Host is trusted for URL generation.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If false, test H3 by adding X-Forwarded-Host instead of modifying Host.

minimal_experiments.experiment: Repeat the same reset/notification trigger, leaving Host unchanged but adding X-Forwarded-Host (and separately X-Forwarded-Server) set to your collaborator domain.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: The generated link's domain reflects the forwarding header even though Host itself was untouched.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: Neither forwarding header affects the generated link.
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Reveals whether an allowlist check on 'Host' is being silently bypassed via a sibling header.
minimal_experiments.next_experiment: If both fail, test whether a caching layer rather than the origin is responsible (H4).

minimal_experiments.experiment: Send a request with a collaborator-domain Host/X-Forwarded-Host to a cacheable path, then send a second, unmodified request for the same resource from a different client/session and inspect its response.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_true: The second, unmodified request receives content influenced by the first (poisoned) request.
minimal_experiments.observation_if_false: The second request is unaffected by the first.
minimal_experiments.information_gain: Confirms whether the vulnerability is a cache-keying gap rather than (or in addition to) direct URL-generation trust.

decision_points.question: Did the generated link's domain change when Host was modified?
decision_points.yes: Proceed to confirm impact via safe token-capture on your own test account.
decision_points.no: Test whether a forwarding header is trusted instead.

decision_points.question: Did a forwarding header change the generated link's domain?
decision_points.yes: Document that the allowlist check on 'Host' does not cover this header.
decision_points.no: Test for a cache-keying gap (H4) using a second, unmodified request.

what_must_be_proven: A client-supplied header value is embedded, unvalidated, into a link or decision that a separate trusting party will act on.
The delivered content plausibly reaches, or is retrievable by, a trust boundary the attacker does not otherwise control.

evidence.evidence: Your own test account's password-reset email arrives with a link pointing to your collaborator domain, and visiting the poisoned link with the leaked token successfully authenticates as that test account.
The generated link's domain changes to your collaborator domain, but you have not yet demonstrated that the resulting token, once captured, actually authenticates the account.

A subsequent unmodified request to a cacheable path returns content that appears influenced by an earlier crafted request, but the causal link to the specific header has not been isolated from other variables.

confirmation.safe_confirmation: Confirm the full chain only against a test account you control: capture the reset token delivered to your own collaborator server, then use it against the real application URL to verify it authenticates the test account. Do not attempt this against another person's account.

capability_and_impact.primitive: The ability to make the server embed an attacker-chosen domain into content it generates or caches, without directly compromising the server itself.

capabilities.capability: Redirect a security-sensitive token to an attacker-controlled domain
capabilities.additional_prerequisite: The victim (or an automated system) must actually click the delivered link.
capabilities.impact: Full account takeover of the affected user if the token is single-use and sufficient to complete a password change.

capabilities.capability: Serve attacker-influenced content from a shared cache to unrelated visitors
capabilities.additional_prerequisite: A caching layer must actually store and later serve the poisoned response to other users.
capabilities.impact: Ranges from defacement to, in severe cases, client-side script execution if reflected unsanitized.

capabilities.capability: Bypass a Host-based access-control or vhost-routing decision
capabilities.additional_prerequisite: A distinct, differently-configured virtual host or routing rule must exist.
capabilities.impact: Access to functionality intended only for a different, more privileged virtual host.

impact_conditions: Whether the leaked token alone is sufficient to complete an account takeover, or whether additional verification is required.
Whether the caching layer's TTL and scope actually cause the poisoned response to reach other real users before it expires.
Whether an automated system will visit the poisoned link before the intended human victim, potentially consuming a single-use token harmlessly.

defense_analysis.defense: Ignore the Host header for URL generation; use a fixed, server-side configured application domain.
defense_analysis.assumption: The application never legitimately needs to serve multiple base domains from the same codebase/config.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: No legitimate multi-tenant or multi-domain deployment requires per-request domain selection.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Multi-tenant SaaS applications often need to generate links for many customer-specific domains, reintroducing exactly the trust decision this defense was meant to eliminate.
defense_analysis.investigation: Check whether the deployment is single-domain or multi-tenant; if multi-tenant, this defense alone is insufficient.

defense_analysis.defense: Validate the Host header against a strict, server-maintained allowlist before using it for anything security-sensitive.
defense_analysis.assumption: Every code path that reads a domain for security-sensitive purposes consults the same validated value, and no sibling header bypasses the check.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, and any other forwarding header are either stripped at the edge or subjected to the identical allowlist check as Host.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: A framework or library helper used elsewhere in the codebase may independently read a forwarding header directly, unaware that a separate allowlist check exists for 'Host' only.
defense_analysis.investigation: Search the codebase for all reads of Host-like headers and confirm each one is gated by the same validation, not just the primary login/URL-generation path.

defense_analysis.defense: Prioritize the absolute-form request-target over the Host header, per RFC 9112, and never fall back to the header afterward.
defense_analysis.assumption: The server implementation correctly and consistently applies this precedence rule everywhere a domain decision is made, including in application-level code.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: Application code does not independently re-read the raw Host header after the web server has already resolved the authoritative target.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Many web frameworks expose the raw Host header directly to application code via a simple accessor regardless of how the request-target was actually formed, reintroducing the trust decision at the application layer.
defense_analysis.investigation: Confirm whether the specific framework accessor used for 'the current host' reflects the RFC-mandated precedence, or simply returns the raw Host header unconditionally.

defense_analysis.defense: Include the effective Host (and any forwarding headers the origin actually consults) in the cache key at the caching layer.
defense_analysis.assumption: The caching layer's configured cache key matches every header the origin's response content actually varies on.
defense_analysis.what_must_remain_true: Cache-key configuration is kept in sync whenever the origin's logic that reads Host-like headers changes.
defense_analysis.how_assumption_fails: Cache-key configuration is often set once at infrastructure-provisioning time and not revisited when application code later starts trusting a new header for URL generation.
defense_analysis.investigation: Compare the caching layer's configured cache-key headers against every Host-like header actually read by the origin's URL-generation and routing logic.

common_misconceptions.misconception: If the Host header doesn't affect which page loads, the application isn't vulnerable.
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Routing and URL generation are separate trust decisions. An application can correctly route based on a validated Host while still trusting an unvalidated forwarding header for link generation.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: Test each Host-like header against each security-sensitive use independently — a pass on one does not imply a pass on the others.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Only the literal 'Host' header matters; forwarding headers are an implementation detail.
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Server are conventions, not enforced standards — any application behind a reverse proxy may read them, and many allowlist checks target only 'Host'.
common_misconceptions.correct_model: Enumerate every header the target application might plausibly consult for 'the current domain', not just Host.

false_positives.observation: Changing the Host header appears to change a link in the response, but the link was already present in static page content unrelated to your request.
false_positives.incorrect_conclusion: The application dynamically reflects the Host header into URL generation.
false_positives.why_incorrect: The observed link may be a coincidental match, a cached artifact, or hardcoded content that happens to resemble the injected value.
false_positives.what_to_verify_next: Use a distinctive, unique collaborator domain so any reflection is unambiguous, and confirm the effect reproduces across fresh, uncached requests.

failed_attempts.attempt: Sent a password-reset request with a modified Host header and expected the reset link's domain to change immediately.
failed_attempts.result: The reset link still pointed to the real application domain.
failed_attempts.why: The application used the request-target's absolute-form or a fixed configuration value rather than the Host header for link generation.
failed_attempts.lesson: A single negative result on 'Host' does not rule out the mechanism; forwarding headers and cache-keying gaps must be tested as distinct hypotheses.

variants.name: Direct Host header trust in URL generation
variants.condition: The application reads the Host header directly and uses it, unvalidated, to build absolute URLs.
variants.mechanism_detail: No forwarding header or caching layer is involved; the trust failure occurs entirely within the origin's own URL-construction logic.
variants.investigation_difference: Simplest case: modifying Host alone is sufficient to test the hypothesis.
variants.how_to_identify: Change Host and observe whether any generated absolute URL reflects it.
variants.how_to_confirm: Trigger a link-generating flow on a test account and confirm the token/link reaches your collaborator domain.

variants.name: Forwarding-header bypass (X-Forwarded-Host / X-Forwarded-Server)
variants.condition: A reverse proxy sits in front of the origin, and the origin trusts a forwarding header the proxy is assumed — but not guaranteed — to control exclusively.
variants.mechanism_detail: An allowlist check may validate 'Host' while a separate code path reads X-Forwarded-Host directly.
variants.investigation_difference: Requires testing each forwarding header independently, since Host alone may show no effect.
variants.how_to_identify: Add X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Server headers and check for divergent behavior.
variants.how_to_confirm: Confirm the specific header name the vulnerable code path actually reads, then reproduce the effect using only that header.

variants.name: Cache-key mismatch (web cache poisoning via Host)
variants.condition: A caching layer's response varies based on a Host-like header, but the cache key does not include that header.
variants.mechanism_detail: The poisoned response is stored and later served to a separate, unrelated visitor requesting the same cached path.
variants.investigation_difference: Requires a second, independent request to confirm the poisoned entry is actually served to someone else.
variants.how_to_identify: Send a request with a modified Host-like header to a cacheable path, then issue an unmodified follow-up request.
variants.how_to_confirm: Reproduce reliably across multiple follow-up requests from a genuinely separate network path.

transfer.shared_mechanism: mechanism.trust-boundary-confusion — attacker-controlled input is trusted as authoritative for a security-relevant decision without independent validation.

related_topics.shared_principle: Both rely on a privileged component acting on unvalidated, attacker-supplied data — SSRF via the server's network position performing a fetch, Host header attacks via the server's content-generation or caching authority producing trusted-looking output.
The cache-key-mismatch variant of Host header attacks is a specific instance of the general cache-poisoning pattern.
OAuth redirect_uri validation can suffer an analogous failure when a client-supplied value is trusted without allowlist confirmation.

transfer.transferable_reasoning: Whenever a system reads client-supplied metadata and uses it, without independent validation, to decide 'who am I talking to' or 'what should I generate/serve', the same investigation applies: does the value reach a security-sensitive decision, and is there any code path that reads it before the intended validation?
new_contexts: Multi-tenant SaaS platforms generating tenant-specific links or subdomains from request metadata
Serverless/edge-function deployments where multiple 'Host-like' signals can disagree
GraphQL or API gateways that construct absolute URLs in response payloads from request headers
Single-page applications that trust a server-generated bootstrap value built from the Host header

sources.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy — Password reset poisoning
sources.claim: Documents password reset poisoning as an attacker manipulating a website into generating a password-reset link pointing to an attacker-controlled domain, by controlling the Host header used to build that link.

sources.title: IETF RFC 9112 — HTTP/1.1, Section 3.2.2 (request-target)
sources.claim: Specifies that when a request-target is in absolute-form, an origin server MUST ignore any received Host header field and use the host information from the request-target instead.

sources.title: Django Security Advisory — Host header poisoning (django.http.HttpRequest.get_host())
sources.claim: Documents that Django's Host header parsing in affected versions mishandled userinfo-style syntax, allowing an attacker-controlled domain to be used to generate arbitrary URLs.

claims.statement: When a request-target is sent in absolute-form, an origin server MUST ignore any received Host header field and instead use the host information from the request-target.
claims.scope: HTTP/1.1 as specified by RFC 9112; applies to compliant origin servers and proxies processing absolute-form request-targets.

claims.statement: An attacker can cause a website to generate a password-reset link pointing to an attacker-controlled domain by manipulating the Host header used to construct that link, then capture the reset token when the victim (or an automated system) follows the link.
claims.scope: Applications that dynamically construct absolute URLs for password-reset or notification emails from the Host header (or a trusted forwarding header) without independent server-side validation.

claims.statement: An application may validate the literal 'Host' header against an allowlist while a separate code path reads a forwarding header (X-Forwarded-Host or X-Forwarded-Server) unvalidated, allowing the allowlist to be bypassed via the sibling header.
claims.scope: Deployments behind a reverse proxy where the proxy does not strip or overwrite client-supplied X-Forwarded-* headers before forwarding, and application code independently consults these headers.

claims.statement: Django's Host header parsing (django.http.HttpRequest.get_host()) in the affected versions incorrectly handled userinfo-style syntax in the Host header (e.g. 'validsite.com:random@evilsite.com'), allowing an attacker-controlled domain to be accepted and used to generate password-reset URLs.
claims.scope: Django versions affected by this historical parsing defect, prior to the corresponding framework-level fix; illustrative of a broader class of Host-parsing implementation bugs rather than a claim about current Django behavior.

claims.statement: If a caching layer's response content varies based on a Host-like header but the cache key does not include that header, a request bearing a manipulated header value can cause a poisoned response to be stored and later served to unrelated visitors requesting the same cached path.
claims.scope: Caching layers (CDN or reverse-proxy cache) placed in front of an origin whose response construction reads a Host-like header that is excluded from the configured cache key.

claims.statement: A client MUST send a Host header field in an HTTP/1.1 request even when the request-target is in absolute-form, to preserve compatibility with older HTTP/1.0 proxies that may not process absolute-form targets.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Given a request/response pair, identify whether a client-controllable header is reflected into generated output that a separate party will later trust.
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Learner correctly names the specific header and the specific output it influences, without being told in advance that a header is involved.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Design a minimal, safe experiment to test whether a suspected header-trust gap actually changes application-generated output.
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Proposed experiment isolates the header as the only changed variable and specifies what result would confirm vs. rule out the hypothesis.

learning_objectives.observable_action: Distinguish a primitive from a proven impact.
learning_objectives.success_criteria: Learner explicitly identifies what additional fact is required before claiming real-world impact.

scenarios.title: Multi-tenant workspace invite links
scenarios.context_domain: A B2B SaaS product where each customer organization has its own workspace, reachable via a company-specific subdomain.

prompt.setup: A collaboration platform lets any employee invite teammates by entering an email address. The platform sends an invite email containing a link back to the workspace. The engineering team mentions, almost in passing, that the invite-link domain is 'derived from whatever the browser's request said it was talking to, so it works correctly no matter which of our regional edge domains the admin happened to load the app from.' The platform sits behind a shared reverse proxy that forwards all traffic to a single pool of application servers, and does not modify or strip any client-supplied metadata about the original request.
prompt.task_question: What capability, if any, does an attacker gain here, and what would you need to establish before claiming it results in account compromise of an invited teammate?

expected_reasoning.invariant_analysis: A value used to determine 'which domain does this invite link point to' must reflect the platform's real, intended origin — not an arbitrary value the requester's browser happened to send.
expected_reasoning.boundary_analysis: The trust boundary is between the client's own request metadata (fully attacker-controlled) and the domain embedded into content that a separate person — the invited teammate — will later read and click.
competing_hypotheses: The application ignores request-derived domain metadata entirely and uses a fixed, server-configured domain per workspace instead.
The application reflects a client-controllable value directly into the invite link with no independent validation.
The application validates one specific header for this purpose, but a different, related header used by the same code path bypasses that validation.
The described behavior only affects which regional UI the admin's own browser loads, and does not affect the domain embedded in emails sent to other people at all.
expected_reasoning.minimal_safe_experiment: Using a test workspace and a test invite address you control, trigger the invite flow twice: once normally, and once while modifying the relevant client-supplied header (or its likely forwarding-header sibling) to a domain you control. Compare the resulting invite email's link domain across both attempts.
expected_reasoning.capability_calibration: Observing the invite link's domain change demonstrates only the primitive. It does not prove account compromise: that additionally requires a real invited teammate to click the link, the link to carry a sensitive token, and no additional verification step between clicking and gaining account access.
expected_reasoning.remaining_uncertainties: Whether the invite link actually carries a sensitive, single-use token determines whether this primitive has any real impact at all; that must be confirmed from the invite email's actual contents, not assumed from the domain-substitution result alone.

scoring_rubric.description: Can the learner state what should have determined the invite link's domain, and what determined it instead?

levels.0: Learner cannot articulate any expected guarantee about the invite link's domain.
levels.1: Learner vaguely states 'the link should be correct' without identifying what makes it correct.
levels.2: Learner identifies the domain should be the platform's own, but not what source of truth should determine it.
levels.3: Learner correctly states the domain should derive from a server-controlled, validated source.
levels.4: Learner additionally identifies the specific failure: trusting request-supplied metadata as if it were that validated source.

scoring_rubric.description: Can the learner locate where untrusted, request-time data crosses into content a different, later party will trust?

levels.0: Learner does not distinguish the attacker's own request from the invited teammate's later action.
levels.1: Learner notes 'the email is sent to someone else' without connecting it to a specific data source.
levels.2: Learner identifies the invite email as the delivery point but not the specific header/metadata source.
levels.3: Learner correctly identifies the client-supplied header as the untrusted input crossing into the emailed link.
levels.4: Learner additionally notes the shared reverse proxy detail as relevant to which specific header is exploitable.

scoring_rubric.description: Are the learner's candidate explanations mutually exclusive and each independently testable?

levels.0: No alternative hypotheses offered; jumps straight to 'it's vulnerable.'
levels.1: One hypothesis offered, untested against alternatives.
levels.2: Two hypotheses offered but they overlap or aren't independently distinguishable.
levels.3: Several distinct, testable hypotheses offered.
levels.4: Hypotheses additionally include a 'no real effect' explanation, guarding against over-eager confirmation.

scoring_rubric.description: Does the proposed experiment isolate the variable of interest while minimizing risk to real users?

levels.0: No concrete experiment proposed.
levels.1: Experiment proposed but would affect a real, non-test teammate or workspace.
levels.2: Experiment uses a test account but changes multiple variables at once.
levels.3: Experiment isolates a single header change using a test workspace/invite address.
levels.4: Experiment additionally anticipates testing the forwarding-header hypothesis as a distinct follow-up.

scoring_rubric.description: Does the learner separate 'the server will embed my value' from 'this results in account compromise'?

levels.0: Learner treats any domain reflection as automatic full compromise.
levels.1: Learner asserts impact without naming any additional required condition.
levels.2: Learner names one additional condition needed but not others.
levels.3: Learner names multiple additional conditions.
levels.4: Learner explicitly states the impact conclusion is unproven until the invite link's actual token/content is inspected.

scoring_rubric.description: Does the learner identify what remains unknown rather than presenting a confident final verdict?

levels.0: Learner presents a definitive compromise/no-compromise verdict with no caveats.
levels.1: Learner mentions uncertainty exists but does not specify what is uncertain.
levels.2: Learner names one genuine unknown.
levels.3: Learner names multiple genuine unknowns.
levels.4: Learner ties each named unknown back to a specific next step that would resolve it.

common_learner_errors.error: Concluding the scenario describes SSRF because a server-side value is attacker-influenced.
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: No server-side network request to an attacker-chosen destination occurs here. The mechanism is the same family but manifests as content generation, not a network fetch.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Focus on what capability is actually demonstrated: does the server perform a request to an attacker-chosen destination, or does it embed an attacker-chosen value into content that someone else will trust? These are distinguishable by what the server actually does with the value.

common_learner_errors.error: Assuming that because the domain in the invite link changed, the invited teammate's account is now compromised.
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: Changing the link's domain only proves the primitive. Compromise additionally requires the teammate to click the link, the link to carry something sensitive, and no further verification step to block reuse.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Explicitly separate 'I changed the link's destination' from 'I demonstrated account takeover', and identify the specific missing piece of evidence needed to close that gap.

common_learner_errors.error: Testing only the most obvious header (Host) and concluding the application is safe when it shows no effect.
common_learner_errors.why_it_fails: The scenario's shared reverse proxy detail is a deliberate hint that a forwarding header, not necessarily Host itself, may be the actual trusted value.
common_learner_errors.remedial_guidance: Enumerate the plausible set of Host-like headers a proxied application might read before concluding the pattern does not apply.

diagrams.text:
MENTAL MODEL: Host-Like Headers as Ambient (Unverified) Identity
==================================================================

  Client Request                     Server-side belief
  ---------------                     -------------------
  Host: real-app.com          --->    "This request is for real-app.com"
  (attacker changes to:)
  Host: evil-collab.com       --->    "This request is for evil-collab.com"
                                        (server has no independent way to
                                         confirm this — it takes the
                                         client's word for it)

  If that belief then feeds into:
     - a generated absolute URL (password reset link, canonical link)
     - a cache key / routing decision

  ...the attacker's chosen domain travels into content or decisions that
  OTHER, TRUSTING parties (a victim's inbox, a shared cache) will act on
  — not just into the attacker's own session.

NORMAL vs VULNERABLE
=====================

NORMAL:
  Client Host header ----X (ignored for security-sensitive use)
                          |
                          v
  Server-side fixed config / validated allowlist
                          |
                          v
  Generated URL / routing / cache key uses ONLY the trusted value


VULNERABLE:
  Client Host header (or X-Forwarded-Host / X-Forwarded-Server)
                          |
                          v (read directly, no independent check)
  URL-generation logic / routing / cache-key logic
                          |
                          v
  Attacker's chosen domain now embedded in server-generated
  content or decisions

CAUSAL MECHANISM: From Header to Delivered Content
=====================================================

  [Attacker]
     | sends request with crafted Host / X-Forwarded-Host
     v
  [Origin server / component behind reverse proxy]
     | reads header to decide "which domain is this for"
     v
  [URL-generation / cache-key / routing logic]
     | uses header value directly, no allowlist check
     v
  [Generated artifact]
     | e.g. password-reset link embedded in an email,
     |      or a cached HTTP response
     v
  [Third party — NOT the attacker]
     | a victim's inbox / a future cache visitor
     | trusts and acts on the artifact (clicks link / receives cached page)
     v
  [Security-relevant outcome]
       token leaked to attacker-controlled domain
                  OR
       poisoned content served to unrelated visitors

CAPABILITY CHAIN: Primitive -> Capability -> Impact
======================================================

  PRIMITIVE
  Server embeds attacker-chosen domain into generated
  content / cache entry / routing decision
        |
        | + victim actually clicks delivered link
        v
  CAPABILITY
  Password-reset (or similar) token is delivered to an
  attacker-controlled domain instead of the real app
        |
        | + token alone is sufficient to complete a
        |   password change (no extra verification step)
        v
  IMPACT
  Full account takeover of the affected user

  --- separate branch ---
  PRIMITIVE (same as above)
        |
        | + caching layer stores & later serves the
        |   poisoned response to OTHER visitors
        v
  CAPABILITY
  Poisoned content served from shared cache
        |
        | + poisoned content includes executable/reflected
        |   content, not just a wrong link
        v
  IMPACT
  Client-side script execution / broad content injection
  affecting many unrelated users

THREE VARIANTS OF THE SAME MECHANISM
=======================================

1) DIRECT HOST TRUST
   Host header --------------> URL generation (no proxy involved)

2) FORWARDING-HEADER BYPASS
   Host header ----[validated, blocked]
   X-Forwarded-Host --[NOT validated]--> URL generation
   (allowlist checks the wrong header; proxy doesn't strip the other one)

3) CACHE-KEY MISMATCH
   Request A: Host: evil.com --> origin generates poisoned response
                                       |
                                       v
                            [Cache stores response,
                             cache key does NOT include Host]
                                       |
   Request B (different, unmodified) -+--> same cache entry returned
   from an unrelated visitor               (now poisoned) to them too

concepts.summary: Authentication tokens, session identifiers, and identity attributes that are implicitly and automatically attached by the client runtime (browser or OS) to an outbound request based solely on the target destination, rather than being explicitly and deliberately attached by application logic for each distinct user action.

bounded_scope.covers: Browser-managed session cookies, cached HTTP Basic/Digest authentication, TLS client certificates, Kerberos/NTLM ambient tokens, and the architectural distinction between implicit environmental authority and explicit programmatic authorization.
bounded_scope.delegates: SameSite cookie scoping and browser default policies are delegated to concept.samesite-cookies; cross-origin dispatch boundaries are delegated to concept.same-origin-policy; token-based anti-CSRF synchronizer patterns are analyzed in topic.csrf.

learning_objectives: Distinguish ambient credentials (automatically appended by the runtime environment) from explicit credentials (programmatically supplied by application code).
Trace how the automatic attachment of ambient credentials transforms the browser into an unwitting confused deputy on behalf of untrusted origins.
concepts.mental_model: An ambient credential is like an automated electronic company badge pinned to a messenger's coat. Whenever the messenger approaches the corporate headquarters building, the gate sensor reads the badge and unlocks the doors—without checking whether the messenger was dispatched by the company CEO or tricked by a rival. Because the browser automatically attaches cookies to every request matching the target domain, the receiving server cannot determine whether the request was intentionally triggered by the user or surreptitiously provoked by a third-party website.
concepts.mechanism: When an HTTP request is dispatched from a browser context, the browser inspects its internal credential stores: (1) Cookie Jar: Any cookie matching the target domain and path (subject to SameSite and Secure attributes) is automatically formatted into a 'Cookie: ...' request header. (2) HTTP Authentication: If credentials were provided previously for the realm via HTTP Basic or Digest, the browser automatically injects the cached 'Authorization' header. (3) Client Certificates: If mutual TLS (mTLS) is established, the browser completes the TLS handshake using the local client certificate. (4) Operating System Authentication: On Windows/Active Directory, NTLM/Negotiate authentication headers are automatically negotiated. In all these cases, the user-agent attaches authority implicitly without requiring JavaScript on the originating page to know, handle, or explicitly approve the credential. When a malicious third-party origin induces the browser to issue an HTTP request (via HTML form submission, fetch, image tag, or script), the ambient credential attachment mechanism fires automatically unless explicit cross-site restrictions prevent it.
security_relevance: CSRF: The entire vulnerability class relies on ambient credentials (primarily session cookies) being attached to cross-site requests.
Confused Deputy Problem: The browser acts as an intermediary possessing authority (cookies) that an unauthorized caller (malicious web page) abuses to execute actions.
Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH): WebSocket handshakes automatically include ambient cookies, enabling unauthorized full-duplex socket establishment from malicious origins.

Authorization Architecture: Explains why Bearer tokens stored in non-ambient storage (e.g. in-memory JavaScript variables) require explicit attachment and are inherently immune to classic CSRF, but more vulnerable to XSS.

common_assumptions.assumption: If a request contains valid user session cookies, the user must have intentionally initiated the action.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: The browser attaches cookies automatically based on destination domain matching, irrespective of whether the request originated from the user's intent or an attacker's cross-site script.
common_assumptions.security_implication: State-changing operations without secondary, non-ambient verification (such as anti-CSRF tokens or SameSite=Strict cookies) are vulnerable to forgery.

common_assumptions.assumption: Setting HttpOnly on session cookies prevents CSRF.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript from reading document.cookie (defending against token theft via XSS). It does not stop the browser from automatically sending the cookie on HTTP requests across origins.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Developers believe HttpOnly protects against CSRF, leaving the application completely unprotected against cross-site requests.

common_assumptions.assumption: Requiring POST requests instead of GET prevents ambient credential abuse.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: HTML <form method='POST'> elements automatically submit cross-origin POST requests with full ambient cookies.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Relying on HTTP method switching as a security boundary fails against standard automated form submission payloads.

concepts.summary: How hostnames are resolved to IP addresses, and why the resolution process introduces security-relevant non-determinism — particularly the assumption that a hostname maps stably to the same IP address.

bounded_scope.covers: DNS hierarchical resolution, TTL expiration, caching behavior, and temporal instability between multiple resolution calls (TOCTOU).
bounded_scope.delegates: Network routing and IP reachability are delegated to concept.network-trust-boundaries; URI decomposition is delegated to concept.url-parsing.

learning_objectives: Explain how time-to-live (TTL) expiry permits non-deterministic resolution between validation and connection phases.
Derive why hostname allowlists fail to guarantee IP address safety without resolved IP pinning.
concepts.mental_model: DNS resolution translates a hostname into an IP address. This translation is not guaranteed to be stable: the same hostname can resolve to different IPs over time (TTL expiry, round-robin, geographic routing). When a system validates a hostname at one point in time and connects at another, the two resolutions may return different addresses. This gap is the foundation of DNS rebinding attacks.
concepts.mechanism: When an application resolves a hostname, it queries DNS recursively: local cache → system resolver → recursive resolver → authoritative nameserver. The response includes one or more IP addresses and a TTL (time-to-live) value. After TTL expiry, the next resolution may return a different IP. An attacker controlling a DNS zone can configure extremely short TTLs (e.g., 0 seconds) so that the first resolution returns an innocuous public IP (passing validation) and the second resolution returns a private IP (reaching the internal network). This is DNS rebinding.
security_relevance: SSRF — DNS rebinding bypasses hostname-based validation by changing resolution between check and connect
SSRF — Time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) between DNS validation and HTTP connection
Cache poisoning — DNS cache can be poisoned to redirect resolution
Subdomain takeover — dangling DNS records pointing to unclaimed resources
SSRF — Attacker-controlled hostnames with A records pointing directly to internal IPs (127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254) bypass hostname-based allowlists without needing DNS rebinding or TTL manipulation

common_assumptions.assumption: DNS resolution is stable — the same hostname always resolves to the same IP.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: TTL expiry, DNS rebinding attacks, round-robin DNS, and geographic routing all cause resolution to change between lookups.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: A validate-then-connect pattern may validate against a public IP but connect to a private IP if DNS changes between the two lookups.

common_assumptions.assumption: Validating the hostname is equivalent to validating the destination IP.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: A hostname can resolve to any IP, including private/internal addresses. Hostname validation (e.g., checking against a domain allowlist) does not constrain the resolved IP.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: An attacker-controlled hostname on an allowed domain can resolve to 127.0.0.1 or internal IPs.

common_assumptions.assumption: DNS resolution happens once per request.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Some HTTP clients re-resolve DNS on redirect. A URL may initially resolve to a public IP, then after a redirect, the re-resolution may return a private IP.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF bypass via redirect chains that trigger re-resolution.

concepts.summary: How HTTP redirect responses (3xx status codes) cause clients to issue follow-up requests to a new URL, and why redirect-following behavior introduces security-relevant state changes — particularly when validation occurs before the redirect but the action occurs after.

bounded_scope.covers: HTTP 3xx semantics, Location header processing, client redirect-following policies, and post-validation destination mutations.
bounded_scope.delegates: URL parsing of Location headers is delegated to concept.url-parsing; resolution of redirected hostnames is delegated to concept.dns-resolution.

learning_objectives: Identify how client-side redirect following introduces a gap between initial validation and final request destination.
Explain how open redirects on allowlisted domains can be chained to reach internal destinations.
concepts.mental_model: An HTTP redirect tells a client to make a new request to a different URL. If a server-side HTTP client follows redirects automatically, the effective destination may differ from the originally validated URL. Validation happens on the initial URL; the action (the actual connection) happens on the redirect target. This creates a TOCTOU-like gap where the redirect target can point to a restricted destination that would have been blocked by initial validation.
concepts.mechanism: HTTP status codes 301, 302, 303, 307, and 308 signal redirects. The Location header specifies the new URL. Most HTTP client libraries follow redirects automatically by default. When an application validates a user-supplied URL and then passes it to an HTTP client that follows redirects, the redirect target is not re-validated. The redirect can point to an internal IP, a different scheme (http→file, http→gopher), or a different port.
security_relevance: SSRF — redirects bypass URL validation by changing the effective destination after the check
Open redirect — attacker-controlled redirect chains can send users to malicious sites
SSRF — scheme changes during redirect (http→file, http→gopher) can access non-HTTP protocols
OAuth — redirect_uri manipulation via open redirects to leak authorization codes

common_assumptions.assumption: The URL validated is the URL that will be fetched.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: If the HTTP client follows redirects, the effective destination is the final redirect target, not the initially validated URL.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: Validate http://allowed-host.com which redirects to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

common_assumptions.assumption: Redirects stay within the same scheme.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: A redirect can specify any scheme in the Location header, including file:// or gopher://. However, most modern HTTP client libraries (curl 7.86+, Python requests, Java HttpClient, Node fetch) block cross-scheme redirects by default. This technique is primarily relevant for older library versions or custom HTTP clients with permissive redirect policies.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: Scheme-switching redirects can access local files or interact with non-HTTP services.

common_assumptions.assumption: The application controls the redirect destination.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: An open redirect on an allowed domain lets the attacker control the final destination via the redirect chain.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF filter bypass via open redirects on allowlisted domains.

sources.title: PortSwigger - Bypassing SSRF filters via open redirection
sources.claim: Documents using open redirects on allowed domains to bypass SSRF URL filters

sources.title: OWASP - Server Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.claim: Documents redirect-based SSRF bypass techniques and recommends disabling automatic HTTP redirects or re-validating the redirect destination before following

concepts.summary: How network architecture creates implicit trust relationships — internal networks trust requests from internal IPs, cloud metadata services trust requests from instance IPs, and localhost services trust requests from the loopback interface — and why these trust relationships become exploitable when an attacker can cause a trusted component to make requests on their behalf.

bounded_scope.covers: Positional network trust, ingress/egress firewalls, private RFC 1918 subnets, loopback interface isolation, and cloud link-local metadata (169.254.169.254).
bounded_scope.delegates: DNS resolution of hostnames to network addresses is delegated to concept.dns-resolution.

learning_objectives: Differentiate ambient positional network authority (IP-based trust) from explicit cryptographic authentication.
Map trust boundary transitions in cloud and enterprise architectures (Internet -> DMZ -> VPC -> Localhost -> IMDS).
concepts.mental_model: Network trust is positional: a service decides who to trust based on where the request comes from, not who initiated it. Internal services trust internal IPs. Cloud metadata trusts instance IPs. Localhost services trust the loopback interface. If an attacker can cause a server to make a request, the request arrives from the server's IP — which is trusted — regardless of who actually initiated it.
concepts.mechanism: Network segmentation creates zones of trust. The most common trust boundaries in web applications are: (1) Internet ↔ DMZ — firewalls restrict inbound access. (2) DMZ ↔ Internal network — application servers in the DMZ may have access to internal services. (3) Any host ↔ Localhost — services bound to 127.0.0.1 are only accessible from the same machine. (4) Instance ↔ Cloud metadata — the metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) is accessible only from within the cloud instance. These boundaries are enforced by network position (source IP), not by authentication. When SSRF allows an attacker to make the server issue requests, the requests cross these boundaries using the server's trusted position.
security_relevance: SSRF — the core mechanism exploits the server's network trust to reach internal services
Cloud credential theft — metadata endpoints (AWS 169.254.169.254, GCP, Azure) return IAM credentials to any request from the instance
Lateral movement — internal services often have weak or no authentication because they rely on network position for access control
Localhost attacks — services bound to loopback trust all local connections

common_assumptions.assumption: Internal services are protected because they are not reachable from the internet.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: SSRF makes the application server act as a proxy. The request reaches the internal service from a trusted internal IP.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF: Internal admin panels, databases, and APIs accessible via SSRF without authentication.

common_assumptions.assumption: Cloud metadata is safe because it's only accessible from within the instance.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: If SSRF allows the server to request http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, the metadata service returns IAM role credentials because the request comes from the instance itself.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF to cloud credential theft — one of the highest-impact SSRF attack paths.

common_assumptions.assumption: Network-level access control is sufficient for service protection.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Network-level controls prevent direct external access but do not prevent indirect access via a compromised or misused internal component (SSRF).
common_assumptions.security_implication: Defense-in-depth: internal services should still require authentication, not rely solely on network position.

concepts.summary: The fundamental browser security mechanism that isolates resources across different origins (protocol, host, and port tuple). Crucially, the Same-Origin Policy enforces asymmetric isolation: it strictly blocks cross-origin reading of response data, but historically permits cross-origin sending of requests (such as form submissions, image loads, and simple POSTs), creating the structural prerequisite for cross-site request forgery.

bounded_scope.covers: Browser origin definition (scheme, host, port), DOM tree isolation, XMLHttpRequest and Fetch read-access restrictions, and the distinction between cross-origin writes (permitted) and cross-origin reads (blocked).
bounded_scope.delegates: Cookie attachment rules and cross-site isolation attributes are delegated to concept.samesite-cookies; implicit session credential transport is delegated to concept.ambient-credentials; selective relaxation of read restrictions is delegated to topic.cors.

learning_objectives: Evaluate whether two arbitrary URIs share the same origin by comparing their scheme, host, and port tuple.
Differentiate the Same-Origin Policy's permissive write/send posture from its restrictive read posture to identify why cross-origin state changes succeed.
concepts.mental_model: The Same-Origin Policy is an asymmetric boundary: it is primarily designed to prevent cross-origin reading, not cross-origin sending. If origin A embeds a form targeting origin B, the browser sends the request to origin B (along with B's credentials). However, the browser prevents origin A from reading the response from origin B. Attackers exploit this asymmetry in CSRF: when the target action is a state-changing operation, triggering the action is sufficient to achieve impact—the attacker does not need to inspect the response.
concepts.mechanism:
An origin is defined by RFC 6454 as the tuple (scheme, host, port). Two URLs belong to the same origin if and only if all three components match exactly. The browser enforces this boundary in two primary ways: (1) DOM access: Scripts executing in origin A cannot access the DOM, window objects, or global variables of frames or windows belonging to origin B. (2) Network requests: While XMLHttpRequest and Fetch requests to origin B can be initiated, the response body and headers are withheld from origin A's script unless origin B explicitly permits reading via CORS headers. However, for legacy web compatibility, the browser does not block the dispatch of standard cross-origin network requests (such as HTML
POST/GET, ,
security_relevance: CSRF: Exploits SOP's permissive write behavior where cross-origin requests are dispatched with credentials even though responses cannot be read.
CORS: Mechanisms designed to selectively relax the SOP's read restrictions for authorized cross-origin consumers.
Clickjacking: Overlays transparent frames across origins to trick users into interacting with a protected UI.
DOM XSS: Bypasses SOP entirely by executing attacker-controlled JavaScript directly within the victim origin's execution context.

common_assumptions.assumption: The Same-Origin Policy stops an external site from sending HTTP requests to my application.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: The Same-Origin Policy restricts JavaScript from reading the response of a cross-origin request; it does not stop the browser from issuing the request or the server from processing it.
common_assumptions.security_implication: CSRF: Developers mistakenly assume SOP protects state-changing endpoints from unauthorized external initiation.

common_assumptions.assumption: Enabling CORS headers or configuring CORS properly prevents CSRF.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: CORS is an opt-in mechanism to relax read restrictions for cross-origin AJAX requests. It does not protect against standard HTML form submissions or simple cross-origin requests, which execute before any CORS preflight or response inspection.
common_assumptions.security_implication: False sense of security: Teams implement CORS allowlists thinking they prevent cross-site request forgery, leaving endpoints vulnerable.

common_assumptions.assumption: Subdomains are isolated by default under the Same-Origin Policy.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: While app.example.com and api.example.com are distinct origins, cookies scoped to .example.com are shared across both, and document.domain (legacy) could relax DOM boundaries.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Cookie tossing and cross-subdomain CSRF attacks when cookies lack host-only scoping.

concepts.summary: The cookie attribute defined in RFC 6265bis that controls whether cookies are attached to cross-site requests. By configuring SameSite as Strict, Lax, or None, servers specify the boundary conditions under which ambient cookie authority is withheld or transmitted during cross-site navigations and subresource requests.

bounded_scope.covers: RFC 6265bis SameSite attribute values (Strict, Lax, None), site boundary definition (registrable domain / eTLD+1 plus scheme), top-level navigation exceptions, browser default behaviors (Lax-by-default), and the Chromium 2-minute Lax-allowing-unsafe window.
bounded_scope.delegates: The strict origin tuple (scheme, host, port) is defined in concept.same-origin-policy; the underlying concept of implicit credential attachment is defined in concept.ambient-credentials; full CSRF mitigation architecture is analyzed in topic.csrf.

learning_objectives: Differentiate the transmission rules for SameSite=Strict, SameSite=Lax, and SameSite=None across subresource requests, form submissions, and top-level link navigations.
Identify security vulnerabilities that persist under SameSite=Lax, including state-changing GET requests, top-level navigations, and client-side redirects.
concepts.mental_model: SameSite is a gatekeeper installed on the browser's cookie jar. Before attaching a cookie to an outbound request, the browser compares the origin of the current web page (the initiator) with the destination of the request (the target). If they belong to different 'sites' (eTLD+1), SameSite determines whether the cookie is allowed to leave: Strict forbids it entirely, None allows it completely, and Lax allows it only if the user is actively navigating the browser's top-level address bar using a safe (read-only) HTTP method.
concepts.mechanism: SameSite evaluates requests based on the 'site' abstraction—defined as the public suffix plus one label (eTLD+1) along with the URL scheme (Schemeful Same-Site). The three policy levels behave as follows: (1) Strict: The cookie is never sent in cross-site requests under any circumstance, including when the user clicks an ordinary top-level link from an external email, search engine, or website. (2) Lax: The cookie is withheld on all cross-site subresource requests (e.g., ,
security_relevance: CSRF Defense: SameSite=Lax provides automated baseline protection against cross-site form POST attacks without requiring server-side token validation.

State-Changing GET Vulnerability: Applications that perform sensitive actions via GET requests remain completely exploitable even when SameSite=Lax is active, because top-level GET navigations transmit Lax cookies.
WebSockets (CSWSH): WebSockets are initiated via an HTTP Upgrade request, which is treated as a cross-site subrequest; SameSite=Lax prevents cookie attachment during cross-site WebSocket handshakes.
User Experience vs Security: SameSite=Strict breaks user login continuity when following external links (requiring re-authentication), prompting most web applications to deploy SameSite=Lax.

common_assumptions.assumption: Modern browsers default to SameSite=Lax, so CSRF is dead and no longer needs defensive engineering.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: SameSite=Lax still attaches cookies on top-level GET navigations. Any application endpoint performing state changes on GET (or accepting GET for POST actions) remains vulnerable. Furthermore, mobile webviews, legacy embedded browsers, and older desktop clients do not enforce Lax by default.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Developers drop anti-CSRF token verification on sensitive endpoints, exposing users to trivial GET-based CSRF or mobile webview exploits.

common_assumptions.assumption: SameSite uses the same boundary as the Same-Origin Policy.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: SOP uses the exact tuple (scheme, host, port). SameSite uses 'site' (scheme + eTLD+1). Two subdomains (login.example.com and attacker.example.com) are different origins under SOP, but the same site under SameSite.
common_assumptions.security_implication: If an attacker compromises or hosts content on a subdomain (e.g., via subdomain takeover or XSS), SameSite does not protect against cross-subdomain requests because both subdomains are same-site.

common_assumptions.assumption: SameSite=None is safe if the Secure flag is enabled.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: SameSite=None; Secure ensures the cookie is transmitted over HTTPS, but explicitly re-enables cross-site cookie transmission, restoring the classic CSRF attack surface entirely.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Third-party embedded widgets or federated identity systems using SameSite=None are vulnerable to cross-site request forgery unless protected by anti-CSRF tokens.

sources.claim: Specifies the SameSite cookie attribute, defining the semantic rules and transmission algorithms for Strict, Lax, and None across cross-site and same-site contexts.

concepts.summary: How URLs are decomposed into components (scheme, authority, host, port, path, query, fragment) and why different parsers may disagree on which component contains which bytes.

bounded_scope.covers: Specification-defined URI component decomposition (RFC 3986), character delimitation, authority parsing (userinfo@host:port), and common syntactic disagreements between parsers.
bounded_scope.delegates: DNS resolution of host strings is delegated to concept.dns-resolution; redirect following is delegated to concept.http-redirects.

learning_objectives: Decompose a URL string into scheme, userinfo, host, port, path, query, and fragment per RFC 3986 §3.
Identify syntactic elements ('@', '#', '%', backslashes) that trigger parser disagreements between validators and HTTP clients.
concepts.mental_model: A URL is a structured string. A parser decomposes it into components: scheme://userinfo@host:port/path?query#fragment. Security problems arise when two systems parse the same URL string and disagree about which part is the host, which part is the path, or which part is the userinfo — because a security decision made by one parser's interpretation does not constrain the action performed using the other's.
concepts.mechanism: RFC 3986 defines the generic URI syntax as scheme://authority/path?query#fragment, where the authority component is further decomposed into userinfo@host:port. The '@' character separates optional userinfo from the host. The '#' character separates the fragment. The '/' separates path segments. However, many real-world applications implement ad-hoc URL parsing (string matching, regex extraction, or library-specific parsers) that may disagree with the RFC grammar. Common disagreements include: (1) which part of the URL is the host when '@' is present (the host is AFTER the last '@'), (2) whether '#' terminates the authority or is part of the path, (3) how percent-encoding is handled before vs. after parsing, (4) whether backslashes are treated as path separators, (5) how IP addresses in alternative formats (decimal, hex, octal, IPv6) are resolved.
security_relevance: SSRF — URL parsing disagreements between validator and HTTP client can bypass destination restrictions
Open redirect — parser disagreements about the host component can redirect to attacker-controlled domains
OAuth — redirect_uri validation can be bypassed via URL parsing inconsistencies
Path traversal — path normalization differences (dot-segments, encoding) can escape intended directories
Request smuggling — URL parsing differences between proxy and backend
Web cache poisoning — URL normalization differences between cache and origin

common_assumptions.assumption: Two URL parsers will extract the same host from the same URL string.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Different parsers handle the userinfo '@' separator, fragment '#' delimiter, and percent-encoding at different stages. A validator may see 'expected-host' while the HTTP client connects to 'evil-host' from the same URL.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF allowlist bypass: URL validator and HTTP client disagree about the destination host.

common_assumptions.assumption: Percent-encoding is decoded consistently across components.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: Some parsers decode before splitting components; others split first, then decode. Double-encoding exploits parsers that decode recursively.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Path traversal and SSRF filter bypasses using encoded delimiters (%2f for '/', %40 for '@', %23 for '#').

common_assumptions.assumption: An IP address in a URL unambiguously identifies a network host.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: IP addresses can be represented in decimal (2130706433), octal (017700000001), hex (0x7f000001), IPv6 (::1), or mixed formats. A blocklist checking for '127.0.0.1' will miss equivalent representations. Note: octal notation is supported by glibc (Debian/Ubuntu) but NOT by musl libc (Alpine Linux/Docker), Go's net.ParseIP(), or Python's ipaddress module — effectiveness depends on which resolver the target server uses.
common_assumptions.security_implication: SSRF blocklist bypass via alternative IP representations. Effectiveness varies by runtime — always test against the target's actual resolver.

families.core_principle: Attacker-controlled DATA becomes CONTROL when a parser with a richer grammar interprets it. The security failure occurs because the data crosses an interpretation boundary where its meaning changes from inert content to executable structure.
conditions: Attacker controls input that reaches a parser/interpreter
The parser has a grammar richer than the data was intended to carry
No boundary enforcement prevents the data from acquiring structural meaning
families.investigation_question: Does attacker-controlled input reach a parser that could interpret it as structure rather than content?
families.defensive_implication: Ensure that attacker-controlled data cannot acquire structural meaning in the target grammar — through parameterization, escaping appropriate to the target context, or sandboxed interpretation.

families.core_principle: Two components interpret the same attacker-controlled representation differently. A security decision made using one interpretation does not constrain the operation performed using the other.
conditions: Two or more components process the same input
The components use different parsing rules or specifications
A security-relevant decision is made by one component but the action is performed by another
families.investigation_question: Do two components in the request path interpret the same bytes differently, and does a security decision depend on one interpretation while the action uses the other?
families.defensive_implication: Normalize the representation before making security decisions, or ensure all components in the chain agree on parsing rules.

families.core_principle: Attacker-controlled input causes a privileged component to act on the attacker's behalf, crossing a trust boundary that should separate the attacker from the privileged capability.
conditions: A component has authority the attacker lacks (network position, credentials, file access)
Attacker-controlled input influences what the privileged component does
The trust boundary between the attacker and the capability is not enforced at the input layer
families.investigation_question: Can attacker-controlled input cause a privileged component to perform an action the attacker could not perform directly?
families.defensive_implication: Validate attacker-controlled input against a strict allowlist before passing it to any privileged component. Apply defense-in-depth at the infrastructure layer.

families.core_principle: A security decision uses attacker-influenced identity, object reference, or context, allowing the attacker to access or modify resources they should not reach.
conditions: The application makes an authorization decision
The decision depends on attacker-controllable data (object ID, role, session, token)
The application does not independently verify the relationship between the authenticated identity and the requested resource
families.investigation_question: Does the application verify that the authenticated user is authorized for the specific resource, or does it trust an attacker-controllable reference?
families.defensive_implication: Authorization decisions must use server-side session state and independently verify the relationship between the authenticated identity and the requested resource.

families.core_principle: A security decision depends on state that can change between the check and the use, or the application assumes sequential processing where concurrent processing is possible.
conditions: A security-relevant check and a subsequent action are not atomic
An attacker can influence the state between the check and the action
The race window is reachable in practice
families.investigation_question: Is there a time-of-check-to-time-of-use gap where an attacker can change the state that a security decision depends on?
families.defensive_implication: Make security checks and their dependent actions atomic. Use database-level locking, compare-and-swap operations, or serialized processing where race conditions could affect security properties.

families.core_principle: Data crosses a serialization/deserialization boundary and acquires unexpected authority — either through object reconstruction, prototype manipulation, or type confusion.
conditions: Attacker controls serialized data
The deserialization process can reconstruct objects with side effects or authority
The application does not restrict what types can be deserialized
families.investigation_question: Does attacker-controlled data pass through a deserialization process that could reconstruct objects with authority or side effects?
families.defensive_implication: Never deserialize untrusted data using a general-purpose deserializer. Use allowlists for permitted types. Prefer data-only formats (JSON) over object-graph formats (Java serialization, pickle).

families.core_principle: A browser or client-side component makes a trust decision based on context (origin, referrer, framing, DOM state) that the attacker can manipulate.
conditions: A security decision depends on the request's origin, context, or framing
The attacker can manipulate the context (e.g., by hosting a malicious page that makes cross-origin requests or frames the target)
The application does not independently verify the action's legitimacy
families.investigation_question: Can an attacker manipulate the context in which the user's browser interacts with the application, causing the browser to perform actions or leak data the user did not intend?
families.defensive_implication: Use anti-CSRF tokens, strict CORS policies, X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors, and avoid trusting client-side DOM state for security decisions.
